title: AI Governance as a Strategic Marketing Capability

detail.title: AI Governance as a Strategic Marketing Capability
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has transformed how organizations collect, interpret, and act upon customer information. Yet, marketing theory continues to treat market intelligence largely as a reliable input rather than an organizational output shaped by algorithms, data quality, governance choices, and institutional constraints. This assumption becomes increasingly problematic as customer understanding is delegated to predictive systems whose logic is often opaque to the managers who rely upon them. Drawing on Market Orientation Theory, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the Resource-Based View, and digital strategy literature, the paper develops a governance-enabled framework linking AI governance capability to market intelligence quality, market orientation effectiveness, digital strategy execution, brand trust, and competitive advantage. It also argues that AI governance functions as a strategic marketing capability governing the production, interpretation, and strategic usability of algorithmically generated customer intelligence. Proposing that AI governance enhances sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring processes by improving data integrity, reducing algorithmic risk, strengthening accountability, and aligning AI-enabled decisions with customer value creation, the study contributes to marketing theory in three ways. The paper extends market orientation theory, reframes digital strategy, and conceptualizes AI governance as a customer intelligence governance capability rather than a technical or compliance function. It positions AI governance as the mechanism connecting digital strategy to marketing performance. Additionally, it conceptualizes governance capability as a strategic marketing capability rather than a purely technical or compliance-oriented function. The framework advances a governance-enabled theory of AI-driven marketing strategy and proposes hypotheses for future empirical research.

detail.abstract: This paper presents Part B of the Need Engineering Framework — the applied methodology for practitioners seeking to identify latent needs, validate commercial opportunities, design products that progress through the six stages of the Need Formation Sequence, and build recurrence architecture into their business model. Part B is designed to be read and used independently, while serving as the direct applied counterpart to Part A, which establishes the formal theoretical foundation of the framework. The paper introduces four Digital Need Observation Methods — search query analysis, complaint and forum mining, workaround identification, and behavioral trace reading — each representing an updated equivalent of a traditional qualitative research approach, adapted for the contemporary environment in which behavioral evidence predominantly resides. These methods operationalise the Behavioral Signal Axiom established in Part A, which proposes that observed behavior provides more reliable evidence of genuine need than stated preference. Part B further provides the Need Map template for structuring identified needs into commercial decisions, the Three-Variable Entry Scoring Framework for validating market entry positions, a stage-by-stage design guide for moving users through the Need Formation Sequence from exposure to dependency, a recurrence architecture system grounded in the Recurrence Theorem, and the Need Engineering Audit — a diagnostic instrument for identifying where a product has stalled in the formation sequence and what structural changes are required. The methodology draws on behavioral economics, consumer psychology, and entrepreneurship research, while contributing an original synthesis adapted for practitioners operating in resource-constrained environments, including emerging markets. The framework was first presented publicly on January 25, 2026, at the Founders Lab event in Lagos, Nigeria.

detail.abstract: Financial inclusion and entrepreneurial activity are still one of the most important components for economic transformation in emerging economies, but the fact that structural constraints like limited formal financial system access, cumbersome tax systems, etc. remain stifling to business growth and economic participation are still present. Digital banking systems have been growing much faster and are creating new opportunities to increase access to financial services, lower transaction costs, and encourage entrepreneurial activity, and tax policies have an important impact on business incentives, compliance, and investment decisions. This study is conceptual in nature and explores the consequences of digital banking and tax policies on financial inclusion and entrepreneurial development in emerging economies using a structured review and synthesis of the existing literature. The article discusses the impact of digital banking on the delivery of financial services, in terms of being more accessible, affordable and efficient, and examines the level of impact that supportive or restrictive tax systems have on financial service delivery and entrepreneurial performance. Moreover, the study suggests a conceptual model that shows how digital banking, tax regime, financial inclusion and entrepreneurial growth are interrelated, with financial inclusion playing a mediating role. The findings indicate that better digital financial infrastructure and sound tax policy can support each other to promote entrepreneurship, boost small business involvement, and promote inclusive economic growth. The study provides a conceptual framework as well as implications for policy and practice for governments, financial institutions, and development actors to foster entrepreneurship and economic inclusion in emerging markets.

title: The Enjoyment Paradox: College-Educated Mothers Invest More in Their Children's Learning and Enjoy It Less
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago and

detail.title: The Enjoyment Paradox: College-Educated Mothers Invest More in Their Children's Learning and Enjoy It Less

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-83
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: College-educated mothers invest more time in children's learning than non-college-educated mothers, yet they report substantially lower enjoyment of those same activities. Using purposebuilt survey data from 1,552 mothers of kindergarteners in Chicago Public Schools-the first dataset to measure parental time investment, enjoyment, stated motivations, and well-being in a single sample-we document this enjoyment paradox and trace its internal structure. The raw enjoyment gap is 28 percentage points on a peak-enjoyment measure (10/10) and 0.87 points (0.62 standard deviations) on a continuous scale; it survives rich controls for demographics and psychological barriers. The gap is concentrated among non-employed, above-median-income college-educated mothers, who report the lowest enjoyment and invest less than their employed college-educated counterparts at the same income level, even though non-employment is associated with more investment among less-educated mothers. Below the income median, the pattern reverses. We interpret these findings through a framework suggesting that the hedonic cost of intensive investment falls most heavily on the group facing maximum norm salience without a competing professional identity.

title: The Token Economy: Compute Power, Automation, and the Future of Work in an Ecosystem of Human Labor, Capital, and Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Token Economy: Compute Power, Automation, and the Future of Work in an Ecosystem of Human Labor, Capital, and Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: Compute power has become a first-order economic variable. The cost of processing a token-the elementary unit of information that artificial-intelligence (AI) models consume and produce-has fallen roughly 280-fold in two years, even as the compute used to train frontier models grows almost fivefold per year and the largest cloud providers invest more than half a trillion dollars annually in data centers. By May 2026 a single provider, Google, was processing 3.2 quadrillion tokens per month, a sevenfold annual increase. This paper integrates that emerging token economy with the formal economics of automation. Building on the task-based framework of Zeira (1998) and Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018, 2019), it treats compute as a new factor of production and derives a firm-level automate-or-hire rule in which a task is automated only when its token cost falls below its labor cost. The central contribution is to show that this boundary is non-monotonic: because agentic systems can consume up to a thousand times more tokens per task, the cost of automating a task can rise above the cost of human labor even as unit token prices fall-a mechanism consistent with 2026 reports that AI can cost more than the employees it replaces. The paper connects these results to macro estimates (Acemoglu, 2025), transition scenarios (Korinek & Suh, 2024), and 2025-2026 evidence on adoption, corporate spending, and provider economics, and discusses three scenarios for an ecosystem of human labor, capital, and AI.

title: The Productivity Illusion: Why the World's Largest Technology Investment is Failing to Deliver

detail.title: The Productivity Illusion: Why the World's Largest Technology Investment is Failing to Deliver
detail.abstract: The global economy has invested over $750 billion in artificial intelligence since 2013, with global private AI investment reaching $581 billion in 2025 alone. Corporate leaders, governments, and technology vendors have unanimously promised that this investment will deliver unprecedented productivity gains. This paper argues that those promises are systematically overstated and, in most cases, empirically unverifiable. Drawing on longitudinal productivity data from the IMF, OECD, Bureau of Labor Statistics and World Bank, supplemented by systematic document analysis of major institutional AI surveys spanning 2023 to 2026, this study presents four empirical findings that challenge the dominant productivity narrative at a global scale. First, AI investment and total factor productivity are moving in opposite directions across every major economy simultaneously. Second, experienced workers using AI tools take 19% longer to complete tasks than those working without them yet believe they are 20% faster. Third, 56% of global chief executives report getting nothing from their AI investments yet continue to accelerate spending. Fourth, genuine AI productivity gains are confined to just 5% of enterprise deployments. This paper introduces the Productivity Illusion Framework to explain the three mechanisms sustaining this gap and proposes the Measurement Trap as the self-reinforcing process through which organisations continue investing despite evidence of underperformance. The paper also introduces the Workslop Economy as a new theoretical construct describing the emergent category of AI-generated organisational waste that is consuming the productivity gains AI nominally creates.

title: Night Tourscape, Perceived Risk, and Generation Z's Participation in Urban Night Tourism: Evidence from Vietnam's Night-Time Economy

detail.title: Night Tourscape, Perceived Risk, and Generation Z's Participation in Urban Night Tourism: Evidence from Vietnam's Night-Time Economy
detail.abstract: The night-time economy (NTE) is a distinctive spatiotemporal ecosystem rather than a simple extension of daytime commerce, yet behavioural research rarely positions the urban night at its analytical core. This study extends the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) by integrating Night Tourscape (NTS) and Perceived Risk (PR) to explain Generation Z's intention to participate in Vietnam's NTE. Using survey data from 639 Vietnamese respondents aged 18-29 and PLS-SEM with 10,000 bootstrap resamples, the findings identify NTS as the strongest antecedent shaping attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioural control. Perceived risk does not significantly weaken social pressure to participate, suggesting that social connectivity and FOMO-related motivations may remain influential despite safety concerns. MICOM and PLS-MGA further reveal variation across gender and regional groups, with women appearing more responsive to tourscape-related safety conditions and respondents in developing regions more affected by infrastructural and mobility-related constraints. We propose targeted interventions: gender-sensitive lighting design and closing spatial-equity gaps via night-time transport infrastructure.

title: Invisible to the Machine: Algorithmic Revenue Leakage in the Age of AI-Driven Travel Discovery

detail.title: Invisible to the Machine: Algorithmic Revenue Leakage in the Age of AI-Driven Travel Discovery

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This manuscript presents a theoretical and algorithmic modeling framework utilizing aggregate, publicly available macro-level data. This study did not involve human participants, animal testing, or clinical trials; therefore, formal institutional review board (IRB) ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grants or financial support from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. This study was conducted entirely without external funding.

detail.abstract: This study presents a quantitative risk management framework for hospitality, the first to address a crucial paradigm shift in the distribution of travel services from search-based query interfaces supported by legacy search engines to interfaces that utilize Large Language Models (LLMs) and other forms of AI-based generative models. There is an increasing trend in which travelers rely on conversational travel discovery to filter and book itineraries for various travel services. A number of hotels have already started to receive optimal exposure and thereby high REVPARs from the next generation of search architectures, while others that fail to support semantic optimization on their various metadata are exposed to a hidden form of revenue leakage, which is coined here as Algorithmic Revenue Leakage (ARL). In this study, we investigate how hotels that support machine-readable hotel metadata also enable semantic search within their metadata structures and develop a three-tiered framework to formalize MII, ARL, and ΔGOPPAR. By integrating an empirical structural survey (n = 50 luxury hospitality properties), we demonstrate that severe machine invisibility causes an average drop of 8.4% in direct booking shares, forcing a compensatory reliance on high-commission Online Travel Agencies (OTAs). This distribution shift compresses for e.g. GOPPAR by $11.40 to $24.75 per available room, directly eroding institutional asset valuation and long-term profitability. The paper concludes with an actionable architectural blueprint of the AI Data Optimization Layer (AIDOL), equipping hospitality revenue engineers with strategies to restructure dynamic schemas, enhance semantic footprints, and deploy neural APIs to ensure real-time legibility for autonomous AI crawlers.

detail.title: Impact Of Social Media Influencers On Gen Z Purchase Behavior With Special Reference to Ranchi, Jharkhand
detail.abstract: Influence Marketing Through Social Media has been one of the greatest breakthrough trends that have taken place in the domain of Consumer Behavior, leading to significant changes in the way brands interact with their consumers. The Gen-Z era consists of people born between 1997-2012 and is regarded as the generation of individuals who like to go by the advice of their peers more than any marketing strategy. Though a lot of research work has been carried out on the topic of influence marketing among millennials, particularly in urbanized areas of the West, there is not much research that has been done on the purchasing behavior of Gen Zs residing in Tier 2 cities of India. The current paper tries to fill this void by investigating how social media influencers affect the purchasing behavior of Gen Z in Ranchi, Jharkhand.

publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: The average American woman spends approximately $13.25 per month on menstrual products, amounting to more than $6,000 over her lifetime. Yet despite widespread efforts to eliminate the "Tampon Tax," little is known about whether such policies meaningfully improve affordability and access. This study examines the consumer effects of state-level sales tax exemptions implemented between 2016 and 2019 on menstrual products, focusing on price incidence and purchasing behavior across five U.S. states. The findings reveal substantial price reductions of 0.81% per percentage of tax cut within the first 12 months following policy implementation, indicating that tax savings were largely passed on to consumers. Low-income households increased purchases of quantities and shopping frequency by 0.78% and 0.26% respectively, per percentage tax relief, suggesting improved accessibility and reduced stockpiling behavior, while middle and high-income households reduced purchases prior to the policy and primarily shifted toward higher priced and higher-quality products following its implementation.

detail.abstract: The rapid development of social media in Pakistan has altered the way consumers interact with a brand and how they make purchase decisions, especially in Fast Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) sector. This research is an empirical study of the influence of four main antecedents, such as Social Media Marketing (SMM), Electronic Word of Mouth (E-WOM), Brand Trust (BT), and Brand Image (BI), on Consumer Purchase Intention (CPI) in the Pakistani FMCG industry. The data were gathered utilizing a cross-sectional research design on 222 active social media users via a structured online questionnaire. The SPSS and SmartPLS (SEM PLS) were used to analyze measurement and structural models. The results show that there are strong positive direct relationships between Purchase Intention and Brand Image and E-WOM with Brand Image being the strongest predictor. Nonetheless, Social Media Marketing and Brand Trust do not significantly impact Purchase Intention as hypothesized.

title: When Demand Enhancers Collide: Customer Reviews, Product Returns, and Profit Degradation
affiliations: and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: When Demand Enhancers Collide: Customer Reviews, Product Returns, and Profit Degradation

publicationDetails.journalName: HKUST Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Online reviews and lenient return policies are two central instruments for reducing purchase uncertainty in e-commerce. Reviews help consumers learn from prior buyers before purchase, while returns insure them against mismatch after purchase. Consequently, the dominant marketplace paradigm assumes their joint deployment yields additive, or even synergistic, benefits. However, we show that this rationale can severely break down when informational volatility meets physical congestion. To study this dynamic, we develop a two-period analytical model wherein a monopolist sells a single experience good under four systems: no reviews and no returns, reviews only, returns only, and reviews plus returns. Consumers are fully Bayesian and the seller optimally sets prices in each system. The key operational feature is nonlinear reverse-logistics cost: capturing the "diseconomies of scale" inherent in congested return networks. We show that while reviews and returns can each unilaterally increase profit, their combination under certain conditions generates a severe operational externality: review-induced demand variance is transformed into return-volume variance, which is subsequently penalized by convex return costs. Consequently, the joint system exhibits negative complementarity, resulting in relative profit degradation (performing worse than a single instrument) or absolute profit degradation (performing worse than the no-instrument baseline). We also characterize consumer surplus and social welfare, demonstrating how operational externalities can overturn the traditional benefits of information and flexibility.

title: Explanation Singularity of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): An AIGC Information Adoption Perspective
affiliations: Nanjing University

detail.title: Explanation Singularity of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): An AIGC Information Adoption Perspective

publicationDetails.journalName: Information Matters

detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has rapidly become a common source of advice in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and in everyday decision-making. Yet their black box nature often leaves users uncertain about how outputs are produced and whether they should be trusted. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is widely viewed as a potential remedy. However, research and recent debates suggest an important tension: adding explanations does not always lead to better outcomes. This study addresses a central question for research on human–AI interaction and information science: When do explanations facilitate information adoption, and when do they hinder it?

title: Fiscal Stabilization under Adverse Commodity Terms of Trade: State-Dependent Multipliers and the Role of Investment Subsidies
affiliations: Universidad Alberto Hurtado and Alberto Hurtado University

detail.title: Fiscal Stabilization under Adverse Commodity Terms of Trade: State-Dependent Multipliers and the Role of Investment Subsidies
detail.abstract: This article makes two contributions to understanding fiscal stabilization in commodity-dependent emerging and developing economies. First, using nonlinear local projections on a broad panel of non-advanced economies (1995--2015), we show that fiscal spending multipliers are significantly larger during episodes of deteriorated commodity terms of trade (cToT), providing evidence that expansionary government spending is a more effective stabilization tool precisely when commodity exporters face adverse external conditions. Specifically, when countries are characterized by structurally low cToT, fiscal expansions prevent GDP from declining under fixed exchange rate regimes and raise GDP under flexible ones---with investment increasing and consumption remaining broadly stable. Second, we construct a medium-scale open-economy New Keynesian model to identify the structural elements that could explain this econometric regularity. The two exercises are methodologically distinct---the econometric analysis estimates state-dependent multipliers across structurally different countries, while the model simulates the response to an identified terms-of-trade shock---and should not be conflated. Their complementarity lies in one precise point: the structural model reveals that two elements working jointly are capable of generating the same qualitative pattern documented econometrically---investment rising while consumption remains stable when fiscal policy is effective under adverse cToT conditions. These elements are investment subsidies as the primary fiscal instrument and the recovery valuation hypothesis from behavioural macroeconomics, which posits that households place additional value on macroeconomic recovery following adverse shocks. In economies with capital flows and financial frictions under flexible exchange rates, investment and credit subsidies can effectively stabilize a commodity terms-of-trade decline, as measured by GDP growth and welfare changes. Under a fixed exchange rate, the stabilizing effects are more limited because higher interest rates reduce the welfare gains of optimizing households, so the fiscal strategy requires complementary instruments. ​

detail.abstract: From clothes and hairstyles to fashion accessories, humans use a great range of stylistic elements to express themselves, impress others, demonstrate their individualism, or show that they belong to a group. We present new methods to use images as a high-frequency, granular source for the analysis of cultural change. Despite its central importance as a form of social interaction and self-expression, and a rich body of theoretical work, empirical work on style choices is rare. We measure similarity over time and space, tracking the timing and location of influential style innovations. To illustrate our methods, we systematically exploit data from more than 14 million high school yearbook pictures of graduating US seniors to analyze persistence and change in style. We detect the collapse of high conformity as well as persistence across generations in the late 1960s. Style polarization increases sharply across commuting zones from the 1970s onwards. We also develop a novel measure of style innovation and show that it predicts patenting by cohorts later in life, suggestive of broader societal trends facilitating innovation across a range of domains. Overall, our results highlight the usefulness of images as a source for cultural economics.

title: Analyzing Cybersecurity Readiness and Decision-Making Patterns Among Aviation Industry Leaders in India: A Systematic Review and Gap Analysis

detail.title: Analyzing Cybersecurity Readiness and Decision-Making Patterns Among Aviation Industry Leaders in India: A Systematic Review and Gap Analysis
detail.abstract:
Purpose: This research addresses a significant knowledge gap concerning cybersecurity readiness and organizational decision-making frameworks within India's aviation sector. Despite the sector's strategic importance to national infrastructure and economy, the academic literature insufficiently documents cybersecurity vulnerabilities, regulatory implementation gaps, and leadership response patterns to evolving cyber threats.

Design/Methodology: This study employs a qualitative analytical design through systematic literature review, comparative framework analysis, and case study examination. The research synthesized peer-reviewed academic publications from 2018-2026, analyzed domestic regulatory documents issued by DGCA and CERT-In, examined international cybersecurity standards including NIST CSF, ISO 27001, and ICAO Annex 17, and conducted detailed examination of eight to ten documented cyber incidents affecting Indian aviation entities. PRISMA guidelines informed the systematic literature review process, while structured mapping techniques enabled comparative regulatory framework analysis.

Findings: The research revealed substantial adaptation gaps between internationally recognized cybersecurity frameworks and their implementation within India's aviation regulatory environment. Documented cyber incidents, including the 2022 breach affecting Mumbai Airport's cargo operations and the 2023 ransomware disruption impacting SpiceJet, demonstrate systemic vulnerabilities. Critical barriers to cybersecurity maturity include resource limitations across smaller airport facilities, absence of aviation-specific cybersecurity training curricula, fragmented information-sharing mechanisms between government and private sector entities, and ambiguous regulatory responsibilities regarding operational technology security.

Implications: This study produces the first comprehensive synthesis of Indian aviation cybersecurity literature, establishes baseline readiness assessment metrics, and proposes an adapted cybersecurity readiness framework incorporating aviation-specific operational requirements. The research provides strategic recommendations for policymakers, airport operators, and industry stakeholders to enhance sector-wide cyber resilience.

title: TFUDL-CLEM: A Training-Free Unsupervised Deep Learning Registration Method for Fully Automated Correlative Light and Electron Microscopy

detail.title: TFUDL-CLEM: A Training-Free Unsupervised Deep Learning Registration Method for Fully Automated Correlative Light and Electron Microscopy
detail.abstract: We present a registration strategy that targets cross-modality images of different resolutions. Multimodal registration with reference to the prediction of landmarks is still a very challenging problem. Many model-based predictions and manual identification of landmarks have been studied and explored with the use of supervised methods. Despite the various methods available, they all necessitate some level of human involvement, hindering the swift and automated registration process. Here, we demonstrate the image registration of correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM) images with the precise localization of landmark positions using a training-free, unsupervised neural network algorithm, which can process image sizes up to 11k pixels x 11k pixels, depending on the GPU memory size.

title: Local Scale Invariance and Global Mean Reversion in Firm Employment
affiliations: Idilia Consulting

detail.title: Local Scale Invariance and Global Mean Reversion in Firm Employment
detail.abstract: The distribution of firm sizes is often analysed under the assumption of scale‑free growth, typically formalised as proportional dynamics in firm size or log‑size. While such models have proven useful for monetary variables such as revenue or market capitalisation, their applicability to organisational scale remains less clear.This paper studies the distribution of firm size measured by employment for a global sample of publicly listed firms. Using quantile–quantile diagnostics and tail‑count evidence, we show that employment size is inconsistent with globally scale‑free growth. Instead, the data are consistent with a stationary distribution with a characteristic scale and a thin upper tail.We interpret these findings as the outcome of a mean‑reverting diffusion process in logarithmic employment. Growth appears approximately scale invariant at small and medium organisational sizes, but becomes increasingly constrained at larger scales, giving rise to a restoring drift. The implied dynamics correspond to an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck‑type process and do not require ad hoc truncation to generate stationarity.By contrasting employment with revenue‑based measures of firm size, the analysis clarifies why heavy‑tailed outcomes and upper‑tail firms are frequently reported in the literature despite the absence of scale‑free growth in organisational size. The results suggest that scale‑free growth provides at best a local approximation and that organisational constraints play a central role in shaping firm size distributions.

detail.abstract: Do occupational dynasties reflect the intergenerational transmission of skills or nepotism? We use detailed data on the fighting record of the 18th century Royal Navy to show that sons of navy officers are markedly more successful than non-legacies, outperforming in terms of enemy captures by a third. This performance differential is not due to better equipment or more favorable assignments, and also holds for those whose patron has passed away. We provide evidence for positive selection as a channel through which the outperformance is sustained - sons of successful officers are more likely to join and be promoted in the navy. Consistent with vertical transmission, we use computer vision to analyze facial landmarks from over 1,000 portraits. We find that sons of service inherited traits predictive of greater success in naval warfare.

detail.abstract: This paper exploits the nationwide COVID-19 lockdown in India as an adverse migrant labour market shock. We survey a sample of 1,205 out-of-state migrant workers employing internal migration as a coping strategy, and examine their heterogeneous occupational choices and economic consequences after they return to the home state until 14 months after the lockdown. Our empirical analysis reaches several results. First, in the initial months following the lockdown, more than 70% respondents switched occupations to agriculture, with respondents owning farm land 14% more likely to have switched, while those with more work experience and peer networks were less likely to have switched, and instead awaited resumption of regular work channels. Our respondents also went through a period of prolonged income loss even as some switched to agriculture as soon as they could while some remained unemployed. After travel restrictions relaxed, about half of our respondents migrated again and switched back to their pre-lockdown occupations, but with a distinct drop in income compared to pre-COVID levels, tracing an incomplete V-shaped recovery at the time of our survey in the first quarter of 2022.

detail.abstract: The introduction of next-generation multi-receptor incretin therapies for obesity and metabolic syndromes presents a structural financing dilemma for universal healthcare systems. While clinical value is indisputable, the scale of the eligible population triggers unsustainable budget impact projections, producing severe pricing and reimbursement delays that regularly exceed 600 days within the Spanish National Health Service (SNS). This paper introduces a Pharmaco-Actuarial Framework that resolves this impasse through three integrated mechanisms: (i) a Non-Homogeneous Piecewise Exponential Hazard Model that captures the time-varying, front-loaded nature of gastrointestinal attrition during titration phases; (ii) a Universal Entry Rule that eliminates adverse selection by mandating automatic cohort enrollment under SmPC-defined criteria; and (iii) a multi-agent clearinghouse architecture that translates continuous clinical endpoints into three discrete, contractually enforceable response states. The framework transitions the economic evaluation from a static ICER-which at €42,500/QALY exceeds the SNS willingness-to-pay threshold-to an Expected Net Monetary Benefit (E[NMB]) framework that shifts into positive territory under the outcome-based contract. Simulating a cohort of 1,000 patients, the model demonstrates a net budgetary settlement of €5,283,600, reduced to €5,194,800 under a stress scenario of 50% increased titration attrition. A formal game-theoretic analysis identifies a unique Nash Equilibrium at the (Implement MAA, Risk-Sharing MAA) strategy profile. The stress test reveals a counter-intuitive stop-loss property: as real-world clinical performance degrades, public expenditure decreases, achieving absolute fiscal predictability.

detail.abstract: Mass media often persuades; it can also expand the machinery of repression. We study radio network expansion and political persecution in Stalin's Soviet Union, in the decades leading up to the 'Great Terror' of 1937-38. Greater radio coverage systematically intensified political repression: a one-standard-deviation increase in signal strength is associated with roughly 40 percent more arrests and a 20 percent rise in the execution share among those arrested, with effects that grew over time. For identification, we exploit newly digitized county-level panel data for 1920-1940 and variation in longwave radio signal strength driven by ground-conductivity differences along propagation paths. Additional repression was disproportionately misdirected. Post-Stalin rehabilitation records show that high-signal areas produced substantially more sentences later reversed. Within the security apparatus itself, stronger radio reception reduced recruitment into the NKVD. It also increased the probability that incumbent officers were purged or demoted, consistent with tighter monitoring and escalating internal risk. Mass communication was not only persuasive; it operated as an input into coercive state capacity by lowering the coordination and monitoring costs of repression.

title: Generative-AI Temperature and the Design of Internal Innovation Contests

detail.title: Generative-AI Temperature and the Design of Internal Innovation Contests
detail.abstract: Enterprise generative-AI (GenAI) systems contain an operational design choice—the sampling temperature—that affects the diversity and reliability of AI-generated outputs. This paper examines the same idea in an internal innovation contest rather than in a bilateral principal–agent relationship.

detail.abstract: The relevance of the study is determined by the fact that digitalization of the economy is becoming an important factor in economic growth, therefore, it is necessary to assess the degree of its impact and assess the possibility of including this factor in economic growth models. title: Limits of Algorithmic Pedagogies in Indian Public Education

detail.title: Limits of Algorithmic Pedagogies in Indian Public Education
detail.abstract: Algorithmic pedagogies have become increasingly central to contemporary education systems. They have been instrumental in different fields, such as artificial intelligence, data analytics, and platform-based technologies. These pedagogies are being increasingly integrated into the teaching and learning process across the globe. In this background, public education systems have emerged and are frequently positioned as key sites for algorithmic interventions. The reasons largely pertaining to the scale, administrative reach, and the capacity to generate large volumes of educational data. In this light, policy discourse has been framing algorithmic pedagogies as educational innovations. They have been tabled as having a lot of advantages like improved efficiency, personalized and better learning outcomes. Existing research in this field has been evaluating these systems via indicators like scale, platform usage, engagement metrics, and predictive accuracy. In the context of India, there has been rapid advancements in the integration and adoption of these tools in the education sector. Covid 19 along with National Education Policy (2020) amplified this phenomenon with an intense focus on the deployment of platform-based learning and data driven educational governance like DIKSHA AND SWAYAM initiatives. From learning analytics to automated assessment tools and algorithmic recommendations, there have plethora of innovative interventions in this field. The central argument of the paper is that these evaluations tend to treat these systems as technical tools, while assuming the presence of robust institutions. This over estimation of institutional capacity has made it difficult to capture the macro picture precisely. Here, the meaning and the scope of institutional capacity is not just limited to infrastructure availability, connectivity, or mere teacher training. Rather, it goes beyond to the realms of broader governance which has still remained underexplored. This gap has been more evident in Global South contexts for reasons concerning to institutional heterogeneity, uneven capacity, and complex governance arrangements. These arrangements challenge assumptions which are embedded in dominant models of algorithmic education. 3 This paper attempts to conceptualize algorithmic pedagogies as socio-tech systems that are embedded within public institutions rather than standalone educational technologies. It also contributes to the existing literature that algorithmic pedagogies are primarily governance interventions that recognize authority, accountability and decision making at all levels of public education systems. As a result, making the claim that the effectiveness algorithmic pedagogies ultimately depend on institutional coherence, data governance and sustained organizational learning. Henceforth, reiterating the argument that the limits of algorithmic education are the limits of institutional and governance capacity.

title: Diversification Now, Localization Later: How German SMEs Navigate Battery Supply Uncertainty in the EV Transition

detail.title: Diversification Now, Localization Later: How German SMEs Navigate Battery Supply Uncertainty in the EV Transition
detail.abstract: The shift to electric mobility has reorganized value creation in the German automotive industry around the battery, and in doing so it has exposed firms to supply dependencies that sit largely outside Europe. Most existing research approaches this dependency from the top, focusing on original equipment manufacturers and on EU policy. Comparatively little attention has been paid to the small and mid-sized firms, start-ups, and upstream suppliers that are quietly building the European battery ecosystem from beneath. This paper draws on nine semi-structured interviews with professionals across the German and European battery supply chain, including raw-material producers, component suppliers, battery-technology firms, engineering companies, and an industry observer. It asks how these firms perceive supply uncertainty and how they weigh the two responses most often prescribed: diversification and localization. The findings point to a clear pattern. Diversification is treated as a practical, near-term lever that firms can act on now. Localization is endorsed but treated as a slow, capital-heavy, and politically contingent bet for the future. Chinese dominance of refining and cell production is described less as a threat to be defeated than as a structural condition to be managed. The institutional frictions that mattered most to these firms were not the labor-market rigidities the comparative-capitalism literature emphasizes, but compliance burden, disposal economics, and above all regulatory uncertainty. The paper contributes an upstream, firm-level account of resilience-building and argues that for smaller actors, resilience is built incrementally and under tight constraint.

detail.abstract: Construction aggregate is among the highest-volume mined commodities, yet its low value-to-weight ratio makes it an intensely local market in which the binding constraint is a permitted reserve close to demand. In parallel, hard-rock mining generates very large volumes of waste rock that is, for many host lithologies, geologically equivalent to commercial aggregate but is carried as a reclamation liability rather than as a saleable reserve. This paper asks why geologically equivalent material commands divergent prices across the two markets and why the gap is not competed away. I argue that the dislocation is structural rather than informational, sustained jointly by regulatory separation, capital-allocation asymmetry, geographic-temporal mismatch, and the absence of an intermediating market maker, and I formalize the resulting opportunity as a real option on a physical reserve held by an originating intermediary. Using a stylized parameterization disciplined by published aggregate-pricing and transaction data, I derive the conditions under which the option is accretive to the resource owner irrespective of the eventual aggregate outcome, characterize the convexity of intermediary returns in site quality, and present a sensitivity analysis of assignment value to the aggregate-grade fraction and the development-risk discount. I conclude by identifying the boundary conditions under which the arbitrage compresses and discussing the welfare and policy implications of converting a bonded environmental liability into a productive reserve.

Trusting Interorganizational Networks?
Empirical Relevance and Research Opportunities
detail.abstract: This paper argues that there is an increasing need to trust not only organizations but whole interorganizational networks. That is, there is a strong and growing demand for building what we call 'network trust'. Differentiating between different forms of network governance, applying a practice-based perspective and using the well-known example of the StarAlliance, the paper demonstrates how network trust can emerge within a network, and how external stakeholders, such as customers, suppliers and regulators, can develop trust in a network as whole. Also, we will show that, in turn, network trust can help produce and reproduce trust in single members of a network. The paper concludes with recommendations for future research.

title: An Enhanced Composite Green Logistics Performance Index for MENA: Methodology, Drivers and Hybrid Forecasting to 2030

detail.title: An Enhanced Composite Green Logistics Performance Index for MENA: Methodology, Drivers and Hybrid Forecasting to 2030
detail.abstract: Background: Amid rising trade, urbanization, and carbon emissions in MENA countries, sustainable logistics faces major constraints. This study develops an enhanced Green Logistics Performance Index (GLPI) using min-max normalization and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to integrate the World Bank's Logistics Performance Index (LPI) and Yale's Environmental Performance Index (EPI). The study uses fixed-effects panel regression on data from 20 MENA countries (2018-2024), identifies key drivers, and applies ARIMA and LSTM models for 2030 projections. The prior ratio-based GLPI suffered from scale sensitivity and volatility; this refined version provides improved stability and predictive utility for Green Supply Chain Management (GSCM). Methods: Panel data from 20 MENA countries (2018-2024) were analyzed. The enhanced GLPI normalizes and weights LPI and EPI scores via PCA. Fixed-effects regression identifies drivers, while ARIMA and LSTM enable scenario-based forecasting (baseline, optimistic, and pessimistic). Results: Renewable energy share positively influences GLPI, while trade openness has a negative effect. Projections indicate the regional GLPI will reach about 0.65 by 2030, with Saudi Arabia potentially achieving 25% higher under optimistic conditions. Conclusions: The refined GLPI advances GSCM theory by operationalizing triple bottom line trade-offs through a robust, predictive metric. It bridges descriptive limitations in prior literature, enabling forward-looking insights into sustainable logistics in emerging economies, with potential applicability beyond MENA.

title: The Governance of Two: Ezer Kenegdo, Dyadic Productive Legitimacy, and a Comparative Typology of Foundational Failure

detail.title: The Governance of Two: Ezer Kenegdo, Dyadic Productive Legitimacy, and a Comparative Typology of Foundational Failure
detail.abstract: Institutional theory has neglected the founding dyad as an institutional form in its own right—focusing instead on organizations of three or more while treating the two-person partnership as a social primitive unworthy of systematic theoretical attention. This neglect is analytically costly. The most consequential institutional relationships in human history—the partnerships that founded nations, companies, religious movements, and civilizations—are structured around two actors holding joint accountability for a shared mandate that neither can carry alone. This article argues that the governance dynamics of the founding dyad are qualitatively distinct from those of larger organizations and cannot be derived from them by subtraction. It introduces the concept of Dyadic Productive Legitimacy (DPL)—the condition in which a founding partnership’s cognitive ecology and governance architecture are simultaneously aligned with the shared mandate that gives the partnership its institutional reason for being—and develops a five-mode typology of dyadic governance failure derived from a close reading of Genesis 2–3 as a theoretical source and extended through comparative analysis across nine cases spanning three millennia, four institutional domains, and two scriptural testaments. The five failure modes—Mandate Destabilization, Passive Compliance, Domain Sovereignty Violation, Undefined Governance, and Productive Dissolution—each generate distinct diagnostic predictions regarding failure lead-up, failure moment, and institutional consequence. Genesis 2–3 encodes the foundational architecture of DPL and its two most fundamental failure modes; the comparative analysis extends the typology to three additional modes documented across the full case range. The implications are developed for organizational theory, co-foundership governance, board design, and the methodology of reading ancient texts as theoretical sources.

title:

detail.title:
From Sole Proprietor to Sovereign State: 
Institutionalization, Business Culture, and the Strategic Role of HR Professionals in Nigeria's National Development -A Comparative Study of Nigeria, South Korea, and Singapore 2026
detail.abstract: This paper examines the structural dichotomy between individually-run and institutionalized business enterprises, employing Nigeria, South Korea, and Singapore as comparative frameworks. Anchored in Hofstede's Cultural Dimensions Theory, Chandler's Institutional Theory of the firm, and the Family Business Literature, it argues that Nigeria's historically dominant individually-run business ideology has transcended organizational boundaries and embedded itself within the nation's governance philosophy, policy architecture, and planning culture-producing systemic fragility that mirrors the structural vulnerabilities of founder-dependent enterprises. Through a comparative analysis of South Korea's Chaebol evolution and Singapore's deliberate nation-as-institution model, the paper identifies the cognitive and structural shifts required for Nigeria's institutional transformation. It further positions Human Resource (HR) professionals as the most strategically critical agents of this transformation-serving as cultural custodians, institutional architects, and the primary corridors through which organizational and national values are transmitted, reinforced, and reformed. The paper concludes with a practical framework for HR-led institutional change at the organizational and national level.

title: Supply Chain Management Research in the MENA Region (2000-2025): A PRISMA-guided Systematic Review of Theories, Themes, and Research Gaps

detail.title: Supply Chain Management Research in the MENA Region (2000-2025): A PRISMA-guided Systematic Review of Theories, Themes, and Research Gaps
detail.abstract: Background: Supply chain management (SCM) research has expanded across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), yet the field remains fragmented. Limited synthesis exists on how regional conditions shape research themes, theories, and methods. Methods: This study applies the PRISMA 2020 protocol to review SCM articles indexed in Scopus and Web of Science from January 2000 to March 2025. After screening and eligibility assessment, 512 peer-reviewed studies were retained. Bibliometric mapping and thematic coding were used to identify publication trends, research streams, theoretical lenses, and methodological patterns. Results: SCM research increased sharply after 2015, reflecting national diversification agendas, logistics reform, digitalization, and exposure to global supply chain disruptions. Three dominant streams were identified: resilience, sustainability, and digital transformation. Research output is concentrated in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, while crosscountry comparative studies remain scarce. Empirical studies rely mainly on cross-sectional surveys and SEM-based analysis, with limited longitudinal, qualitative, mixed-method, and comparative work across the region. Conclusions: The study develops an integrative SCM capability framework linking regional structural conditions, capability development, and supply chain outcomes. The findings support managers and policymakers seeking resilient, sustainable, and digitally enabled supply chains, and define clear future research priorities for the MENA region.

title: Analyzing the Likelihood of an Economic Bust in Pakistan: A Study of Key Macroeconomic Indicators
affiliations: University of Central Asia (UCA)

detail.title: Analyzing the Likelihood of an Economic Bust in Pakistan: A Study of Key Macroeconomic Indicators
detail.abstract: Pakistan's economy has long been trapped in a recurring cycle of growth and crisis, driven by persistent fiscal deficits, chronic external imbalances, inadequate revenue mobilisation, and deep-seated structural inertia. This paper employs a hybrid quantitative framework—combining Vector Autoregression (VAR), binary crisis classification via logit and probit models, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA)—to assess the likelihood and precursors of economic busts using annual macroeconomic data spanning 2014 to 2025. The analysis covers eleven key indicators sourced from publicly available official sources, including the current account deficit, fiscal deficit, debt servicing-to-revenue ratio, foreign exchange reserves, inflation rate, and real effective exchange rate. Empirical results identify 2018 and 2022 as systemic crisis years, confirmed by the PCA-derived composite risk index, which captures 47% of total cross-indicator variance. VAR impulse response analysis demonstrates that current account shocks transmit rapidly into reserve depletion and inflation acceleration. Forward-looking projections through 2029 yield low crisis probabilities under baseline assumptions, conditioned on policy continuity. Scenario analysis reveals, however, that reform reversal or an adverse external shock could rapidly reactivate crisis dynamics. The paper concludes that Pakistan's current period of macroeconomic calm constitutes a narrow but critical window for structural reform—one that history suggests is unlikely to remain open for long.

detail.abstract: Wearable technologies now generate continuous, individual-level physiological data about public sector employees, but leadership theory offers little guidance on how managers should interpret and act on those data. This article develops the Performance-Responsive Leadership Framework (PRLF), a conceptual model for the managerial use of human performance information drawn from wearable devices. PRLF integrates four theoretical streams (sensemaking, adaptive leadership, social exchange, and ethical leadership) around three pillars: biometric sensemaking, adaptive decision-making, and ethical integration. The framework extends the public-management literature on performance information use (Moynihan and Pandey 2010; Kroll 2015; Han and Moynihan 2022) to a new class of intimate, continuous, individual-level data, and specifies leader-level mechanisms rather than abstract capacities. The U.S. Army's Optimizing the Human Weapon System (OHWS) program runs through the article as a recurring illustration. The article articulates testable propositions, identifies boundary conditions, and engages three counterarguments (implementation cost, employee privacy, and long-run sustainability) before sketching a research agenda. The contribution is theoretical: PRLF gives public-sector leaders a coherent framework for converting an emerging data stream into responsible managerial action.

detail.abstract: We construct a Crop Vitality Score (CVS) from historical precipitation, temperature, and soil moisture data extracted via the Open-Meteo API for the Punjab cotton belt and demonstrate that this alternative data signal predicts the quarterly earnings performance of Nishat Mills Limited (NML.KA), Pakistan's largest textile conglomerate, with a Pearson correlation of r = 0.80 against excess returns (p = 0.032). Our long-short algorithm, which shorts the textile issuer when August CVS falls below the crop-destruction threshold of 35 and holds the KSE-100 index otherwise, generates an annualized Sharpe ratio of 0.34 and a maximum drawdown of-18.2%. The strategy successfully anticipated the catastrophic 2022 Pakistan floods, avoiding the-17.99% NML decline that followed. These findings suggest that satellite and weather-derived alternative data can penetrate the information opacity that characterizes emerging equity markets, delivering actionable alpha up to 90 days before official 10-Q filings. Our work extends the alternative data literature to frontier market textile sectors and provides a replicable framework for exploiting weather-crop-equity linkages.

detail.title: Improving Customer Satisfaction in Egyptian Customs Clearance Services: The Mediating Role of Blockchain Technology Adoption in the Link between Service Quality and Customer Satisfaction
detail.abstract:
This paper focuses on Egyptian Customs clearance services and investigates the impact of the adoption of blockchain technology on the relationship between service quality and customer satisfaction. The five dimensions of the SERVQUAL model, including reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, and responsiveness, in conjunction with the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework of blockchain adoption, helped guide the collection of data from 401 employees in customs clearance operations. 
      The results of Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with AMOS indicated that the impact of service quality on customer satisfaction is significant (β = 0.495, p < 0.001), while that on the adoption of blockchain is (β = 0.801, p < 0.001). Moreover, the adoption of blockchain positively influences customer satisfaction (β = 0.410, p = 0.003). It was also confirmed that of the relationship between service quality and customer satisfaction (p < 0.001), the adoption of blockchain explains 73.9% of the variance in customer satisfaction (R² = 0.739). 
     The results show that the integration of some blockchain technologies in customs operations can facilitate the service quality and customer satisfaction relationship by enhancing transparency, clearance times, and documentation error. Lastly, this study focuses on the pertinent literature of developing countries in the midst of digital transformation and offers valuable perspective for the Egyptian customs authorities concerned with improving current trade facilitation practices..

detail.abstract: Cash transfer programmes under Nigeria's National Social Safety-Nets Project (NASSP) are among the most ambitious social protection interventions in sub-Saharan Africa. Yet persistent questions remain about beneficiary targeting accuracy, transfer adequacy in a highinflation environment, and community-level accountability. This working paper draws on six years of first-hand field experience as a NASSCO Field Team Leader in Rivers State (2019-2025). The fieldwork covers three key phases: initial NSR enumeration of pilot households in 2019; the 2020 COVID-19 Rapid Response Register (covering 5,000 households); and the 2024 revalidation under the Renewed Hope Initiative with revised N25,000 conditional cash transfers. Over 10,000 households were enumerated across Eleme, Obio/Akpor, and Khana LGAs. Drawing on the COSO Internal Control Framework and Institutional Theory, the paper examines targeting effectiveness, internal controls, and last-mile accountability. Key findings include documentation-driven exclusion errors, PMT miscalibration for South-South livelihoods, verification weaknesses during emergency rollout, and structurally weak grievance redress mechanisms. By mid-2026, the National Social Register had grown to over 20 million households nationally. The paper concludes with practical policy recommendations for strengthening last-mile delivery in Nigeria's cash transfer programmes.

detail.title: Strategic Role of Inspections in Pharmaceutical Supply Chains
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Retailer inspections are the primary mechanism for post-marketing pharmaceutical quality surveillance in developing countries. Resource limitations often mean that retailer detection sensitivity is structurally constrained for certain quality failures, such as excipient adulteration requiring laboratory equipment frequently absent in developing country markets. This motivates upstream supplier inspections such as good-manufacturing-process verification as a policy alternative, but these inspections are resource-intensive and impose compliance costs that may be passed on to consumers. The conditions under which this alternative is effective remain poorly understood. 

Methodology/results: We develop a stylized game-theoretic model: a regulator sets inspection probabilities and noncompliance penalties at the retailer and supplier tiers, two competing suppliers choose quality investment and wholesale prices, and a retailer manages downstream order quantities. We characterize supplier equilibrium conditions and establish three results. First, retailer-and supplier-inspection probabilities are strategic substitutes: increasing inspection intensity in one tier lowers the threshold required in the other to sustain high quality equilibrium. Second, retailer-detection sensitivity, rather than inspection frequency alone, determines whether supplier inspection is the only viable path to a high-quality equilibrium; below a detection-sensitivity threshold, no increase in retailer-inspection probability can attain high quality outcomes. Third, moderate inspection intensities can endogenously sustain asymmetric-quality equilibria among otherwise identical suppliers, where one supplier offers low quality and the other supplier offers high quality. This result offers a new explanation for within-market quality variation, observed in developing countries, beyond cost differences or information asymmetry. We demonstrate how a social planner facing a tension between ensuring medicine quality as well as affordable access may prefer such an asymmetric outcome. An extension to retailer quality investment establishes that upstream and downstream quality investments are strategic complements. 

Managerial implications: Uniform inspection policies across product categories can misallocate limited enforcement resources. We calibrate the model to paracetamol and cough syrup markets in India, demonstrating that structural differences in quality cost and detection sensitivity produce distinct policy prescriptions: existing supplier-inspection frequency suffices for paracetamol, while cough syrup requires a combination of supplier-side enforcement and input-cost subsidies to attain the high-quality equilibrium.

detail.abstract: Cost misperformance, commonly observed as cost overruns, continues to challenge the delivery of transport projects despite advances in estimating, risk management, and oversight controls. The dominant explanation, the Planning Fallacy, attributes overruns primarily to behavioral biases and advocates corrective measures such as reference-class forecasting. Although these approaches have merit, they do not adequately explain why approved cost positions remain difficult to modify as conditions change or why overruns persist even after estimates have been reviewed and refined. Building on the Fifth Hand, a burgeoning theory of project behavior that explains misperformance as a behavioral–institutional outcome arising from interactions between decision-makers and their organizational environments, our paper identifies institutional leadership as the mechanism through which decision environments are designed and maintained. Drawing on ecological rationality, leadership is positioned not as a managerial attribute or additional causal factor, but as the process through which administrative arrangements shape the treatment of uncertainty and adaptation. From this perspective, misperformance arises when changes in design, cost, risk, and delivery information become misaligned with the decision structures governing the commitment, adaptation, and modification of earlier assumptions. Our paper contributes to transport project governance research by identifying the role of institutional leadership in connecting approval and accountability structures to patterns of policy failure and reform drift, an area that remains underexplored in the literature.

detail.abstract: Residential renovation is a credence good: a homeowner can rarely judge whether a quoted price is fair for the work delivered, and the information gap between contractor and client leaves room for overcharging. As general-purpose large language models become a common first point of contact for cost questions, a demand-side question follows: when a homeowner asks plainly, does a model give a usable and verifiable cost basis? This exploratory, reproducible study posed forty residential renovation price questions, phrased as a nonspecialist would ask them, to two frontier general-purpose models (Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-4o) and to a structured cost engine. For each system we recorded the multiplicative width of the returned price range (maximum divided by minimum), whether an explicit overcharge threshold was given, and, for four repeated questions, the sample standard deviation of the width across five runs. The two general-purpose models returned wide ranges, with median widths of about 5 and 15 times and a single run reaching 1,400 times; on repeated runs both models returned a different width almost every time, and the single widest value did not recur. Neither stated an overcharge threshold. The structured engine returned a consistent tiered estimate, an explicit threshold where a per-unit figure applied, and the same output on repeated runs. We do not claim the engine's prices are correct, only that on these questions the general-purpose models did not supply a verifiable basis while a structured layer did. We release the questions, raw outputs, and scoring code.

detail.abstract: Manufactured Deviance Theory (MDT) is introduced as a systems-based theory explaining how deviant identities become reinforced, stabilized, and reproduced through recursive interaction between institutions, social systems, and group adaptation. Existing theories of devianceincluding labeling theory, strain theory, and subcultural theory-provide important explanations for the emergence of deviant behavior and identity but offer limited insight into the mechanisms through which deviant identities persist despite sustained intervention, social stigma, and enforcement pressure. MDT addresses this theoretical gap by proposing that deviant identities are shaped not only by individual choices or group norms, but also by recurring feedback processes linking institutional action, public visibility, social labeling, identity consolidation, and behavioral adaptation. Through repeated cycles of interaction, these feedback mechanisms may unintentionally strengthen group cohesion, amplify symbolic identity markers, and contribute to long-term identity persistence. Drawing on field observations, comparative engagement with sociological theory, and systemsbased analysis, this paper presents MDT as a theory-building framework rather than a fully validated empirical model. The theory is formalized through explicit assumptions, propositions, 2 principles, boundary conditions, and a conceptual feedback-loop mechanism. In doing so, MDT shifts analytical attention from the origins of deviance to the processes through which deviant identities become increasingly durable over time. The paper concludes by outlining implications for sociology, criminology, intelligence analysis, law enforcement strategy, and future empirical research. MDT's central contribution is the proposition that deviance is not merely a characteristic of individuals or groups, but may also be a product of the systems that respond to them.

detail.title: Posterior and Likelihood Sensitivity in Bayesian Distributionally Robust Optimization
detail.abstract: We introduce the notion of worst-case posterior and worst-case likelihood sensitivity. These measure, respectively, the sensitivity of the expected cost to worst-case perturbations of the posterior distribution and worst-case perturbations of the likelihood of a Bayesian model. Each defines a quantitative measure of robustness. A decision maker concerned about the sensitivity of the out-of-sample expected cost to deviations from her assumptions will want a decision for which both sensitivities are small. We derive posterior and likelihood sensitivities for uncertainty sets defined in terms of deviation measures. Posterior sensitivity vanishes when the posterior variance shrinks to zero, which occurs when parameter uncertainty is eliminated from learning. Parameter learning does not eliminate likelihood sensitivity. A distributionally robust formulation of a Bayesian optimization problem makes a near-Pareto-optimal tradeoff between performance (expected cost) and robustness (posterior and likelihood sensitivity).

title: Broadband Access and Adolescent Fertility: Evidence from Rejected Applicants to the 2009 Federal Broadband Stimulus

detail.title: Broadband Access and Adolescent Fertility: Evidence from Rejected Applicants to the 2009 Federal Broadband Stimulus
detail.abstract: A policy-induced rural broadband expansion lowered adolescent fertility, and the response appears to operate through the information and opportunity set rather than through new clinical capacity. Using the funded-versus-rejected applicant margin of the 2009 federal broadband stimulus, the Broadband Initiatives Program (BIP) and the Broadband Technology Opportunities Program (BTOP), as a natural experiment, I compare 2,448 funded counties with rejected-applicant controls trajectory-matched on their strictly-pre-award (2000-2010) population trajectory. A broadband award reduced the rural teen birth rate by about 1.6 per 1,000 in the pre-COVID 2018-2019 window, roughly 3 percent of the 48.6 pre-period baseline and about 11 percent of the teen-birth decline in funded counties. The response concentrates in counties with a Title-X family-planning clinic, a contrast robust to county size and suggestive of broadband amplifying access to existing capacity; young women also appear to complete more schooling, while the adult labor-market response is weak. This information-andopportunity-set margin, rather than the clinical service itself, distinguishes the result from the direct family-planning-access interventions in the literature. The estimate is robust to permutation inference, a staggered-adoption difference-indifferences estimator, and dropping any single state, and remains negative under partial-identification pre-trend bounds, surviving moderate deviations from parallel trends.

detail.abstract: Appearance-based inequality shapes who gets hired, who gets treated, who gets loved, and who gets erased. It is a primary stratification system whose consequences have been systematically underestimated-comparable in structure and consequence to race, class, and gender, yet almost entirely absent from the frameworks built to study them. That absence is not accidental. It reflects structural patterns in how inequality is defined, measured, and prioritised, patterns that have kept appearance off the research agenda, out of the funding conversation, and invisible in policy. This paper names those patterns directly. It examines the three fields that have come closest to this territory-psychology, social epidemiology, and disability studies-and shows precisely where and why each has stopped short. It provides a concrete, cost blueprint for the Global Appearance Inequality Index (GAIIx): the measurement programme the field does not yet have. And it closes with direct demands to researchers, funders, policymakers, the AI industry, and people living with visible difference. This is not an invitation to further study. It is a demand for reckoning.

detail.abstract: Objective Siblings of children with disabilities constitute an often-overlooked target group within care. The serious game ‘Broodles’ has been developed to support them. This study focuses on the motivation and experiences of users, and factors that influence the implementation of the game within special education, health‑care, and welfare organisations.Methods A mixed‑method design was applied. Data were collected through usage data retrieved from the game and an initial and evaluation questionnaire among those interested in the game. Additionally, interviews were conducted with professionals from seven organisations to investigate facilitators and barriers for implementation guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. Two adult siblings reflected on these findings.Results In the first year after the release of the game, 349 individuals created an account. The initial questionnaire was completed by 298 respondents (70 children, 81 parents, and 143 professionals, 4 others) and the evaluation questionnaire by 48 respondents (10 parents, 34 professionals and 4 others). Interviews revealed facilitators, such as the game’s low‑threshold accessibility and having ambassadors, and barriers, such as lacking time to explore and offer ‘Broodles’ to siblings and uncertainty about who is responsible for supporting siblings.ConclusionThis study identified facilitators and barriers of the implementation of ‘Broodles’. title: The Addictive Revenue Trap: State Fiscal Dependency, Corporate Profit, and the Political Economy of Social Harm

detail.title: The Addictive Revenue Trap: State Fiscal Dependency, Corporate Profit, and the Political Economy of Social Harm
detail.abstract: This paper introduces and develops the Addictive Revenue Trap (ART) as a concept drawing on fiscal sociology, institutional economics and political economy, exploring the structural conditions under which states become fiscally dependent upon revenues derived from harmful, habit-forming commodities. The ART observes a self-reinforcing cycle wherein state reliance on sin tax revenues generates regulatory capture, which expands corporate political power, which in turn drives increased consumption of addictive products, whose health and social costs create further fiscal pressure, deepening dependence on the very revenues that perpetuate the harm. The trap’s distinctiveness lies in the addictive property of the commodity generating the revenue, addiction that operates at biological, psychological, and economic levels simultaneously, creating feedback loops that distinguish this trap from ordinary regulatory capture. In formalizing these feedback mechanisms, the paper introduces a continuous-time macroeconomic model of the state’s Net Fiscal Position, mathematically demonstrating how public social expenses are structurally bound to the physical volume of the addiction. Through illustrative case studies of tobacco taxation in the United States, alcohol excise dependence in post-Soviet Russia, and gambling lottery taxation in United States and United Kingdom jurisdictions, the paper demonstrates how the ART operates across diverse institutional contexts. The analysis reveals the moral distortion at the trap’s core, in that the state’s “helping” functions (funding cancer treatment, addiction rehabilitation, and public health initiatives) become justification for perpetuating the very harms the interventions address. The paper concludes by articulating a heterodox policy agenda designed to break the ART’s feedback loops through: decoupling public finance from addictive commodities via functional finance; implementing disinterested management systems for production; democratic corporate charter redesignation; sovereign wealth fund mechanisms with phase-out schedules; civic assemblies to break regulatory capture; and international coordination to prevent regulatory arbitrage.
