detail.title: Multi-dimensional Assessment of Eating behaviour in the Hungarian Adult Population: Motivations, Health–taste Attitudes, and Eating Styles using TEMS, HTAS, and TFEQ-R21
detail.abstract:
Background and aims: Eating behaviour patterns are fundamental determinants of chronic disease risk and public health. Hungary faces among the highest rates of obesity, cardiovascular disease, and diet-related mortality in Europe. Despite this, population-level consumer profiling based on validated multi-scale instruments remains limited. This study aimed to conduct a simultaneous, nationally representative assessment of eating motivations, health and taste attitudes, and eating styles among Hungarian adults, and to derive actionable consumer segments for each dimension.

Methods: Two independent nationally representative cross-sectional surveys were conducted: (1) eating attitudes (TFEQ-R21) and health/taste attitude scales (HTAS) were assessed in 2021 (n =1000); (2) eating motivations (TEMS) were assessed in 2020 (n = 1000). Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) were applied to each instrument. Consumer segmentation was performed using hierarchical and K-means cluster analysis. Sociodemographic differences across segments were explored via chi-square tests and one-way ANOVA. The perceived palatability and healthiness of functional food categories were examined across TFEQ- R21 segments.

Results: The TEMS yielded eight eating motivation factors and five consumer segments: Traditional Simplifiers (17.9%), Frugal Social and Emotional Eaters (19.9%), Balanced Self- Rewarders (27.5%), Health-Conscious (18.3%), and Indifferent (16.4%). The HTAS health subscale produced four clusters, with Health-Conscious Metropolitans (19.8%) as the primary
functional food target. The HTAS taste subscale identified Taste-Oriented consumers (26.9%) alongside three further groups. The TFEQ-R21 confirmed a three-factor eating attitude structure (Emotional Eating, Uncontrolled Eating, Cognitive Restriction; explained variance 57.2%) and yielded five behavioural clusters. Controlled Dieters represented only 20.6% of the adult

population; approximately 75–80% exhibited indifferent, uncontrolled, or emotionally driven eating patterns. Perceived palatability and healthiness of functional foods were significantly higher among Controlled Dieters than other segments (p < 0.05).

Conclusions: The parallel application of three validated eating behaviour scales provides a comprehensive consumer landscape for Hungarian adults. The dominant eating patterns — habitual, taste-driven, and indifferent — along with the limited reach of health-conscious behaviour, underline the urgent need for differentiated public health and food marketing strategies tailored to each segment's psychological profile.

title: Compression Chains and Source-Access Failure: A Conditional Framework for Error-Correction Under Finite Cognition

detail.title: Compression Chains and Source-Access Failure: A Conditional Framework for Error-Correction Under Finite Cognition
detail.abstract: This paper gives a regime-neutral account of a specific failure mode in public cognition: source-starved compression chains can preserve coordination while losing the capacity to correct their own distortions. The argument starts from finite cognitive capacity, a task-relative source-complexity scope condition, non-neutral compression objectives, and the data-processing inequality. Its central distinction is between source-injecting errorcorrection, denoted M5 s , and coherence-only error-correction, denoted M5 c. Coherence checks can improve consistency, decoding, and usability below an information ceiling; only source access can lift that ceiling. Mutual information and task-relative fidelity are kept distinct: the former bounds what a downstream layer can recover, while the latter describes which retained information survives selection. The empirical layer is separated into five numbered premises: P1, fidelity-decoupled or fidelity-adverse selection; P2, counterfeitable provenance cues; P3, channel-specific calibration lag; P4, maintenance-cost asymmetry; and P5, effective chain collapse. The paper does not rank regime types, does not claim that contemporary publics are always chains, and does not offer a predictive model of collapse. It identifies the conditions under which public inputs become source-starved enough for the chain model to apply, and it specifies where the framework can be empirically broken.

title: The Floor Is Fuel: Opposition, Victory, and the Metabolism of Ideological Collapse

detail.title: The Floor Is Fuel: Opposition, Victory, and the Metabolism of Ideological Collapse
detail.abstract: Ideologies usually describe themselves as affirmative projects: visions of justice, order, dignity, nation, equality, freedom, or salvation. This essay argues that affirmation often supplies ideological content, but opposition supplies ideological form. A political disposition can exist before it has a name, programme, or stable boundary. It becomes definite when it encounters an object it cannot tolerate. Opposition is therefore not merely one theme among others inside ideology; it is the nucleating event through which latent inclination becomes public shape. The initial image of crystallization must then be corrected. A crystal, once formed, no longer needs the seed that started it. Ideological form is different. It persists only while some potential difference continues to run through it. Ideology is better understood as a dissipative structure: a pattern maintained under throughput, like a flame, whirlpool, or convection cell. This model distinguishes the boundary of identity from the conditions of its persistence. It also explains why victory is dangerous. When an ideology wins, it does not end opposition; it becomes the largest available object of opposition. The gradient relocates onto the victor. Not every victory vanishes into the next cycle. Some defeated prohibitions precipitate into a floor: norms, taboos, and institutional constraints that later actors inherit rather than contest. But floors are metastable, not guaranteed. They can re-dissolve under pressure and become fuel again. The essay treats this recurrence across three scales as a formal homology rather than an empirical identity: individual crystallization, movement mobilization, and regime succession share a structure, but their observable variables differ. It then applies the model to material delivery, identity delivery, party-system change, civic and ethnic nationalism, and totalitarian collapse. Its central diagnostic is not moral preference but metabolic dependence: a nourishing identity can sustain itself without continuously destroying constraints; a steroid identity must keep producing enemies and consuming the floor in order to feel strong.

detail.abstract:
Purpose

The maritime industry is increasingly under pressure to cut greenhouse gas emissions while preserving the efficiency of global trade operations. This paper analyzes the effects of alternative energy use and operational efficiency on the carbon intensity of different ship classes. The research uses the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) 2023 Ship Fuel Oil Consumption Database to examine how far low-carbon fuels, especially liquefied natural gas (LNG), can take the maritime transport sector toward clean and efficient energy use. The study also explores whether fuel transition patterns vary considerably by vessel type and operating architecture.

Design/Methodology/Approach

A multi-ship-type case study focusing on fuel efficiency was adopted. A quantitative case study technique was used, utilizing aggregated operational and fuel-consumption data from reports submitted by 28,620 ships through the IMO Data Collection System (IMO, 2024). In this study, the relationships between fuel composition, carbon emissions, fleet size, and operational efficiency indicators such as the Annual Efficiency Ratio (AER) were examined using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and one-way ANOVA.

Findings

The results show that containerships, bulk carriers, and tankers account for the largest shares of global maritime fuel consumption and carbon emissions. LNG carriers showed the highest level of alternative fuel adoption, with LNG representing a substantial portion of their fuel mix. Statistical analysis revealed a negative correlation between LNG use and carbon intensity, indicating that shifting toward cleaner fuels can significantly reduce emissions. The study also identified clear differences in energy efficiency among ship categories, with cargo fleets generally being more efficient than passenger and specialist vessels in terms of both fuel economy and operational carbon intensity.

Practical Implications

The study highlights the need for targeted decarbonization policies in the maritime industry. Instead of adopting a one-size-fits-all approach to sustainability, policymakers and industry stakeholders should implement ship-type-specific strategies that promote fuel switching, technical modernization, and operational optimization. Investments in LNG infrastructure, low-carbon fuel systems, and cleaner propulsion technologies can significantly enhance the environmental performance of global shipping.

Originality/Value

This paper contributes to the growing body of literature on maritime sustainability by providing an empirical, data-driven assessment of fuel transition trends based on recent IMO operational records. Unlike purely conceptual discussions on maritime decarbonization, this research offers statistical evidence on the relationship between alternative fuel adoption and the operational carbon performance of different ship categories. The findings provide practical insights for policymakers, maritime operators, and sustainability experts working toward the transition to low-carbon shipping.

title: De-localizing the Local Impacts of Trade through Migration: Evidence from Vietnam

detail.title: De-localizing the Local Impacts of Trade through Migration: Evidence from Vietnam
detail.abstract: This paper uncovers a novel channel of the gains from trade that are spatially propagated across the local labor markets through the pre-existing internal migration network. Using the 2001 U.S-Vietnam Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA), I provide a theory and devise an empirical counterpart to argue for an important contribution of the migration-induced spillover effect from the BTA shock in (i) facilitating the structural transformation away from agriculture and toward industrialization, (ii) improving earnings among the low-educated workers, and (iii) narrowing the skill premium. Importantly, the direct effect of trade on labor reallocation nearly doubles when controlling for the spillover exposure. Further analysis on household spending and regional poverty shows that both direct and spillover exposures improve per capita expenditure for households with low-educated head and effectively reduce poverty incidence, albeit with some differential timing over the short and mediumrun. In particular, while the direct effect reduces regional poverty immediately after the BTA implementation and quickly subsides in the subsequent years, the spillover effect gradually builds up over time and only turns significant by 2008.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Compound Disadvantage of Dwelling Types Within Cape Town Suburbs

detail.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Compound Disadvantage of Dwelling Types Within Cape Town Suburbs
detail.abstract: The persistence of spatial inequality in South African cities is a direct legacy of the country's colonial and Apartheid past. Approaches to analyse such within-city inequalities have conventionally focussed on contrasting historically advantaged neighbourhoods to erstwhile segregated township areas, which were, by design, kept poorer in terms of access to economic opportunities as well as social goods and amenities. This paper uses the city of Cape Town, and the recently released Cape Town Household Survey 2024, as an illustration of how one can add to extant literature by looking within suburbs, and offer a more nuanced understanding of spatial inequality across the city, from its advantaged suburbs (e.g., Southern Suburbs, Atlantic Seaboard) to the disadvantaged township areas in the Cape Flats (e.g., Mitchell's Plain, Khayelitsha). The survey's stratified design separately samples formal dwellings, additional dwellings informal (ADI, commonly known as backyard dwellings), and informal settlement households within the same suburb. Using this within-suburb variation, the paper presents a Compound Spatial Disadvantage (CSD) index combining three dimensions (basic service deprivation, exposure to negative shocks, and spatial confinement) and decomposes inequality in this index within and between Cape Town's 163 surveyed suburbs. The spatial confinement dimension refines conventional amenity-gap measures by using the absolute level of city-wide facility use as a proxy for effective spatial citizenship, which is the capacity to engage with the city as a whole rather than one's immediate neighbourhood. Estimates suggest that this capacity is uniformly low across Cape Town, and that measured differences in compound disadvantage are driven primarily by service deprivation. The paper finds that 61.7 per cent of total CSD variance lies within suburbs rather than between them, and that informal settlement households exhibit a mean CSD of 0.54 against 0.32 for formal households citywide. ADI and informal settlement households in ostensibly well-serviced suburbs face disadvantage levels comparable to those in the poorest townships. These findings indicate that suburb-level averages mask a city-wide (informal) housing crisis that reproduces spatial disadvantage independently of location, with direct implications for targeted service delivery and housing policy.

title: Orientational Residue: How Unrepaired Injuries Become Portable Political Grievance

detail.title: Orientational Residue: How Unrepaired Injuries Become Portable Political Grievance

detail.abstract: This paper asks how a specific social injury becomes portable political grievance. The central claim is that some unrepaired injuries leave behind a low-information, target-specific negative orientation-orientational residue-that can persist after detailed memory of the originating event has thinned. The framework distinguishes three objects often conflated: event-memory (what is remembered), orientational residue (the stance transmitted), and activated narrative (the story later generated under stress). Its load-bearing claim is asymmetric decay: factual content of an injury narrative is costly to maintain and tends to erode, while a target-specific interpretive prior is cheaper to transmit and may persist. Persistence depends on social carriers-language, family transmission, institutions, place, and reinforcing contact-and on carrier density rather than geographic concentration. The framework's strong portability claim is intergenerational: orientation can travel across people who did not directly experience the original injury and attach to later grievances against the same kind of authority. Cross-domain travel across structurally different target types is presented as a related hypothesis, not as demonstrated. Two origination paths are distinguished: injury-derived residue, which skeletonizes through erosion, and mythic or constructed injury narratives, which are assembled for transmission. The article distinguishes acute political entrepreneurship, which converts fresh grievance into rapid political consequence, from latent entrepreneurship, which operates on residue decades later. The framework specifies scope conditions, observable indicators, evidentiary tiers, and falsifiers. Empirical anchors illustrate components of the mechanism with differing evidentiary status, ranging from fullmechanism cases to exploratory applications. The contribution is to specify how political contagion can occur without uniform exposure: a transmissible orientation that makes later stresses feel newly predictive of old expectations.

title: Perpetual War as an Institutional Configuration: Threat Maintenance, Proxy Selection, and Anchor-Indexed Time

detail.title: Perpetual War as an Institutional Configuration: Threat Maintenance, Proxy Selection, and Anchor-Indexed Time
detail.abstract: Perpetual war is often described as a strategy, an economic arrangement, a security discourse, a juridical exception, or a psychological attachment to conflict. Each description can possibly capture part of the phenomenon, but none by itself specifies the configuration by which non-resolution becomes institutionally selectable. This working paper treats perpetual war as a self-reproducing institutional arrangement in which threat-processing is retained more reliably than threat-resolution. The configuration can emerge without design. Once established, it is sustained by proxy metrics-budgets, operational activity, career advancement, doctrinal fit, political blame-avoidance, industrial lock-in, and security-guarantor legitimacy-that are satisfied by managed threat and threatened by arrival. We then link this selection mechanism to anchor-indexed time. Finite agents do not merely persist; they must inhabit the present as legitimate, meaning structurally admissible as a basis for continued agency. Legitimacy span names the temporal bandwidth by which an identity-constituting anchor can carry displacement before restoration, substitution, or collapse becomes compulsory. Because agents carry layered anchors, legitimacy span is vectorial rather than scalar. Perpetual war becomes durable when a threat is routed to a deep shared anchor and security is re-anchored to an unreachable standard such as invulnerability or "never again." The result is a dual temporal geometry: the threat anchor becomes narrow-span, triggering rapid restoration against ambiguous danger, while principle anchors become wide-span, permitting prolonged drift from law, proportionality, constitutional restraint, and declared political ideals. The paper specifies the mechanism, observable implications, exit conditions, and falsification conditions for this configuration.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the institutional implications of central bank digital currency (CBDC) adoption in Central Asia through a detailed comparative study of Kazakhstan's digital tenge pilots and Uzbekistan's digital sum roadmap. Employing the conceptual framework of "algorithmic institutionalism," the study investigates whether CBDC implementation functions primarily as a domestic policy instrument or as a driver of convergence toward supranational digital monetary standards promoted by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Based on policy documents, central bank reports, pilot data, technical standards, and empirical indicators from 2025-2026, the analysis reveals the emergence of algorithmic governance, where programmable monetary features and algorithmdriven compliance mechanisms increasingly shape regulatory practice and potentially constrain discretionary flexibility. The findings indicate that while CBDCs offer notable benefits in transparency, reduced corruption, and improved public expenditure management, this process may simultaneously involve trade-offs, such as architectural alignment with global technical protocols (ISO 20022, BIS unified ledger protocols). This alignment tends to result in a partial erosion of regulatory autonomy and drives a reprioritization of human capital competencies toward operational and technical roles. The paper contributes to debates on monetary sovereignty and digital governance by developing algorithmic institutionalism as an analytical framework for understanding the interplay between technological infrastructure and state authority in emerging economies.

title: How Bitter Is the Pill?State-Dependent Sacrifice Ratios in a Small Open Economy: Evidence from Türkiye
affiliations: Sabanci University

detail.title: How Bitter Is the Pill?State-Dependent Sacrifice Ratios in a Small Open Economy: Evidence from Türkiye
detail.abstract: The cost of disinflation is not a fixed number: it depends on the inflation regime, the credibility of policy, and the open-economy channels through which monetary tightening affects prices. Using monthly Turkish data from 2006 to 2026, this paper studies this state dependence through a state-dependent Phillipscurve framework. I show that the Phillips curve is statistically flat in low-inflation periods, making the implied sacrifice ratio effectively uninformative. In high-inflation periods, however, the inflation-slack relationship becomes much steeper, implying an unemployment sacrifice ratio of about 0.4-0.7 percentage points of the unemployment-rate gap per percentage point of disinflation. Residualized Phillips curves and expectations-augmented specifications show that this steepening is not simply driven by inflation persistence, expectations, or imported costs. The results suggest a conditional view of disinflation: the early phase may be relatively cheap when credibility stabilizes the exchange rate and lowers inflation expectations, but the cost can rise if services inflation, dollarization, indexation, and FX balance-sheet risks keep inflation persistent even as activity slows.

title: The Topology of Economic Fragmentation: Semantic Anti-Agglomeration and Structural Lock-ins in the South African Labour Market
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Topology of Economic Fragmentation: Semantic Anti-Agglomeration and Structural Lock-ins in the South African Labour Market
detail.abstract: Structural transformation, defined as the continuous relocation of labour and capital across economic sectors, remains the primary driver of long-run development and regional prosperity. In contemporary settings, multiple rapid technological transitions occur simultaneously, rendering broad macro-statistics increasingly insufficient for capturing the granular shifts in industrial evolution. To address this gap, recent literature in economic complexity characterises economies as networks where the proximity of industries captures shared productive capabilities, skills, and technologies. This paper operationalises a "genotypic" variant of this perspective by using Sentence-BERT transformers to compute pairwise semantic similarity directly from official industrial classification descriptions, creating a high-resolution "Semantic Space". Projecting sectoral employment data onto this semantic space allows us to view the labour market as networks at different levels of sectoral and spatial aggregation. While theory suggests that growth should propagate along semantically proximate edges through localised knowledge spillovers, cities of the global South face a structural transformation paradox: the sectors that grow do not appear to draw their nearest industrial neighbours along with them, even when those neighbours share deep operational and cognitive similarities. This paper examines that paradox empirically in the South African context, testing whether the near-zero semantic autocorrelation of labour market transitions observed at the national level is, as theory would predict, an artefact of spatial aggregation that dissolves when the analysis is disaggregated to the municipal and intra-city scales. We find that spatial disaggregation fails to surface the predicted positive autocorrelation, with the semantic Moran's I shifting toward more negative values-from +0.004 nationally to-0.035 at the intra-city scale. These results reveal a structural feature we term "semantic anti-agglomeration," where semantically proximate sectors systematically diverge in employment growth due to competitive substitution, structural lock-in, and extreme spatial fragmentation. Such findings demonstrate that in highly unequal urban systems, physical and semantic proximity are doubly decoupled: conceptually adjacent industries fail to co-locate, and even when they do, institutional barriers prevent them from translating that proximity into shared dynamics. Ultimately, this research implies that standard cluster-based industrial policies are unlikely to function without first addressing the underlying urban substrates-such as transport and housing-that allow economic geography to become economic opportunity.

title: Priced in or Passed Through? Carbon Intensity and the Cost of Debt in European Electric Utilities, 2015-2024

detail.title: Priced in or Passed Through? Carbon Intensity and the Cost of Debt in European Electric Utilities, 2015-2024
detail.abstract: I examine whether carbon intensity is priced into the implied cost of debt of European electric utilities over 2015-2024. Using a hand-matched panel of 30 listed firms (174 firm-year observations) and a two-way fixed-effects design that absorbs all time-invariant firm characteristics and aggregate macro-financial shocks, I find that lagged log Scope 1 carbon intensity is associated with a statistically insignificant and imprecisely estimated change in the implied cost of debt (β = 0.0096, cluster-robust SE = 0.018, 𝑝 = 0.59). The result is robust to seven alternative specifications, including a forwardintensity placebo. The point estimate is similar in magnitude to the 26 bp per-standard-deviation carbon premium documented in euro-area corporate bonds (de Jonge, Broeders, and Rijsbergen, 2025), but the cluster-robust standard error yields a 95% confidence interval that spans both zero and literature-sized effects. The most plausible reading is that sector-specific homogeneity in transition-risk exposure within an EU ETS-exposed sector compresses the within-sector variation that lenders would otherwise price; the design's modest statistical power nevertheless means this interpretation cannot be cleanly separated from a literature-sized within-sector premium that the sample is too small to detect.

detail.abstract: Does the increasing automation of the workplace weaken labor unions? The dominant hypothesis in current political economy research is that automation weakens unions and, as a result, undermines worker voice in democratic politics. However, the standard economic theory of automation does not consider unions, and recent political science studies focus on estimating average effects. We argue that the relationship between automation and organized labor is heterogeneous. We integrate task-based automation into a model of strategic worker mobilization and collective bargaining. Our new model suggests that automation can disempower but also empower unions. Empirically, we use quantile instrumental variable regression and find that the impact of robotization on unionization significantly varies across regional labor markets in the US. Consistent with the theoretical perspective, this heterogeneity is mostly due to unobserved characteristics. Our results suggest that research on the political economy impacts of automation should pay more attention to strategic worker mobilization.

detail.abstract: This study was carried in Elgadarif state (central Sudan) with the objective to explore the effect of climate variability on adaptation and mitigation of the different sectors. A questionnaire was carried for key persons experienced in the different fields as agriculture, rangelands, livestock, water etc. Meteorological data for rainfall, temperature and relative humidity were obtained from a Meteorological station in the area. The results showed that despite positive ecological signals, field discussions identified persistent challenges in rangeland degradation, livestock management, water governance, agricultural productivity, and food security. Meteorological analysis showed a slight but statistically significant cooling trend (-0.087 °C per year, p < 0.05), a moderate increase in rainfall (+2.79 mm per year, p < 0.05), and a strong upward trend in relative humidity (+0.76 % per year, p < 0.001). Correlation analysis confirmed inverse relationships between temperature and humidity, and a positive association between rainfall and atmospheric moisture. Collectively, these trends suggest gradual climatic stabilization and improved environmental conditions across the region. Effective adaptation requires integrated land-use planning, institutional strengthening, community participation, and the application of climate-smart agricultural and water management practices. It is concluded that the synergy of remote-sensing indicators and meteorological data underscores the potential for sustainable resource management and enhanced adaptive capacity under changing climate conditions.

title: Against the Public Ownership Conception of Shared Property
affiliations: West Virginia University - College of Business & Economics

detail.title: Against the Public Ownership Conception of Shared Property
detail.abstract: The Public Ownership Thesis is a Kantian-Rousseavian model of shared property. Its advocates argue that it is a superior model to those that can be derived from Lockeanism insofar as private property and common property cannot realise the distinct values that publicly owned property can. Resources that are sites of shared activities must be owned by the public as a whole, on this view. I argue that the various values ascribed to public ownership can be realised by common property on the Lockean model, and that the Lockean model is also better at dealing with the challenges of scarcity and disagreement that are central to questions of property rights.

detail.abstract: This paper provides an analytic characterization of the speed of convergence under learning to a rational expectations equilibrium (REE) for a large class of multivariate models. We show that learning is slower when people's beliefs about model outcomes are more self-fulfilling. The paper also investigates which features of a model economy make beliefs more self-fulfilling, using variants of the simple new-Keynesian model and a medium-scale DSGE model. For empirically plausible specifications of these models, convergence of a learning equilibrium to the REE is so slow that analysis based on rational expectations can be misleading.

title: Multi-Temporal Land Use/Land Cover Change and NDDI-Based Drought Assessment in Semi-Arid Gadaref State, Sudan (1985-2022)

declarations.ethicsApproval: the research deals with remote sensing for changes in natural resources through years

detail.abstract: This study investigates land use and land cover (LU/LC) dynamics in three semi-arid Sudanese localities-Elsefia, Al-Khayari, and Aliadedat-over the period 1985-2022, using multitemporal Landsat imagery processed in Google Earth Engine (GEE) and ArcGIS Pro. The Normalized Difference Drought Index (NDDI) was derived alongside NDVI and NDWI to assess concurrent drought severity across the study period. Results reveal a consistent decline in rangeland across all sites (-2.5% to-4.7%), accompanied by sharp increases in settlement and agricultural areas. Settlement expansion was most pronounced in Al-Khayari (+10,861%), while agriculture surged in Elsefia (+33,350%) and Aliadedat (+527%), reflecting intensified cultivation and urban encroachment. Flooded vegetation expanded significantly in Elsefia (+296%) and Al-Khayari (+173%), suggesting hydrological variability and ecological adaptation. Bare land trends were mixed, with slight declines in Elsefia and Al-Khayari but localized increases in Aliadedat. These findings highlight a regional transition from natural rangeland toward human-dominated landscapes, driven by demographic pressures, agricultural intensification, and climate variability. The study underscores the need for integrated land management strategies-including community-based rangeland restoration, water-efficient agriculture, and evidence-based urban planning-to balance human development with ecological sustainability in semi-arid Sudan.

title: Capital Controls and Credit Reallocation: Evidence from Informal Dollar Liquidity

detail.title: Capital Controls and Credit Reallocation: Evidence from Informal Dollar Liquidity
detail.abstract: We study how changes in Chinese households' effective capital outflow constraints may transmit to U.S. credit markets through bank funding and portfolio choice. Our empirical design uses time variation in an informal U.S.-dollar liquidity channel available to some Chinese households, proxied by national fentanyl seizure volumes. We compare the responses of Chinese-affiliated community banks, which disproportionately serve Chinese-American depositors, with those of other banks. We find that increases in the liquidity proxy are associated with larger deposit inflows at Chinese-affiliated banks. These inflows are accompanied by expansion in residential mortgage lending and a decline in commercial small business lending. Taken together, the results are consistent with a mechanism in which changes in access to offshore dollar liquidity are associated with shifts in the composition of bank credit in destination communities, shifting lending toward residential mortgages and away from small businesses.

title: The Architecture of Par: Run, Redemption Gates, and the Backstop That Selects the Peg

detail.abstract: Under the GENIUS Act and the OCC's proposed implementing framework, a payment stablecoin would hold one-to-one segregated high-quality reserves, redeem within two business days, and be bankruptcyremote. We ask whether such compliance makes par a unique equilibrium, and show that it does not. In a global-games model of redemption, a fully reserve-solvent issuer can suffer a run in which secondarymarket par collapses, and no finite private arbitrage selects par under aggregate stress, because arbitrage capital is state-contingent and withdraws with the run. Only a credible, legally precommitted reopening mechanism-paired with ex ante loss allocation and a risk-taking constraint-selects par. We then show that a redemption gate is not instrument-invariant: it can stabilize under simultaneous redemption but amplifies runs under continuously observable settlement, because it destroys the option value of waiting. Gates are therefore not substitutes for a reopening authority; under continuous settlement they increase the need for one. Reading the GENIUS Act and the OCC's 2026 proposed rule through this lens, we find a framework that materially improves reserve adequacy, redemption predictability, and operational continuity, yet leaves the equilibrium selection of secondary-market par only partially resolved.

title: Information Provision and Demand-Side Barriers to Healthcare Innovation: Experimental Evidence on Shared Medical Appointments in Menopause Care
affiliations: School of Economics, University of Edinburgh, University College London, University of Oxford, University of Virginia - Department of Economics and London Business School - Department of Management Science and Operations

detail.title: Information Provision and Demand-Side Barriers to Healthcare Innovation: Experimental Evidence on Shared Medical Appointments in Menopause Care
detail.abstract: Alternative care delivery models may offer benefits to patients and providers, but adoption often remains low. We study whether brief narrative testimonials shift willingness to attend virtual shared medical appointments (SMAs), a relatively little-used care format in which 5-15 patients with a shared non-urgent health condition meet simultaneously with a clinician. Using a pre-registered field experiment with over 4,000 women aged 45-60 in the UK, we randomly assigned participants to view only standard descriptive information about menopause appointment options (the control group) or to receive testimonials about SMAs from either previous patients or a clinician (treatment groups). Testimonials more than doubled the share of women choosing an SMA: when appointments were offered with a 6-8 week wait, 11% of the control group chose an SMA compared to 26% in the peer testimonials arm and 24% in the clinician testimonials arm. Shorter waiting times further increase uptake. When the SMA wait was reduced to one week, the share of women ever choosing an SMA rose by 14-19 percentage points across arms, reaching nearly 40% in the testimonial groups. Treatment effects are systematically larger among women with greater information-processing capacity: university education, higher baseline menopause knowledge, and broader information-seeking. Our findings suggest that women's reluctance to choose SMAs is driven primarily by demand-side barriers, including unfamiliarity and uncertainty about their benefits, rather than deep-seated aversion to group-based care. Testimonials appear sufficient to meaningfully reduce these barriers.

title: Rules, Not Rulers: Verification, Selection, and the Spatial Distribution of Public Goods in India

detail.title: Rules, Not Rulers: Verification, Selection, and the Spatial Distribution of Public Goods in India
detail.abstract: The distribution of public goods has traditionally been viewed as a function of political power, which concentrates facilities in large settlements and leaves peripheral villages underserved. In this paper, I argue that spatial distribution depends equally on bureaucratic allocation rules. Rules guaranteeing a facility to all qualifying settlements disperse provision, while rules rationing scarce facilities among competitors concentrate it. I test this using school provision in India, exploiting variation within the same elected councils: elementary schools are allocated via an inclusive verification rule, whereas middle schools face competitive selection. Holding governance and demand constant, I find that facility placement across 364,478 villages diverges by 27.1 percentage points depending on the rule applied. Private schools, facing identical demand but no bureaucratic rules, exhibit no such divergence. Expanding the analysis to all 11 public goods in the Indian village census confirms that goods allocated through verification are less concentrated at the center than those distributed via selection or the market. By extending elementary schools to 47,409 peripheral settlements and 54.7 million people, verification rules fundamentally reshape the geography of development. Access at the margins of the state depends less on who governs than on how its rules are written.

title:
Signal Distortion, Adaptive Preferences, and Aggregate Productivity 
A General Equilibrium Theory of Gender-Based Misallocation

detail.title:
Signal Distortion, Adaptive Preferences, and Aggregate Productivity 
A General Equilibrium Theory of Gender-Based Misallocation
detail.abstract: I develop and estimate a general equilibrium model with sector-specific capital in which gender-specific signal distortion generates persistent misallocation, amplified by endogenous price feedback. Women observe returns filtered through a compound discount lambda = lambda_info * lambda_struct(phi), where the structural component -- capturing discrimination and network exclusion -- is endogenous to female participation phi. With sector-specific capital, the wage premium in the modern sector is itself endogenous: women's withdrawal reduces capital accumulation there while raising it in the traditional sector, compressing the premium and making the distorted signal even less likely to trigger entry. I prove that the steady-state preference gap is strictly larger in GE than PE through three distinct channels (signal distortion, wage compression, capital reallocation); unconditional transfers widen the gap by raising the traditional-sector capital stock; the tipping point for self-sustaining convergence is higher with endogenous prices; and the competitive equilibrium is constrained Pareto inefficient due to a triple externality. The preference persistence parameter rho, structurally estimated from Global Findex micro data covering 93,000 respondents across 97 economies, is rho-hat = 0.80 (SE = 0.046), implying an annual half-life of approximately three years for the aspiration gap and confirming the model's geometric preference-decay structure. At estimated parameters, calibrated TFP losses range from 5% to 25% across 58 countries, with a median of 10.8%; Bolivia loses 13.4% and India 19.2%, accounting for 32-48% of the total misallocation in Hsieh and Klenow (2009). A one-time intervention pushing female participation past the GE tipping point generates permanent TFP gains whose present value exceeds intervention cost by a factor of 8-15.

detail.abstract:
This dissertation examines whether commercial orbital insurance systems can operate 
legitimately, sustainably, and within the rule of law where governments — particularly those of 
the Five Eyes intelligence alliance (the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia, 
and New Zealand) — allegedly possess materially relevant classified aerospace information 
unavailable to private risk institutions. The thesis advances four original doctrinal constructs: (i) 
Classified Asymmetrical Risk, the condition in which sovereign actors hold actuarially material 
information withheld from regulated insurance markets; (ii) Planetary Actuarial Instability, the 
resulting incapacity of orbital insurance and reinsurance systems to price catastrophic exposure; 
(iii) Disclosure-Dependent Risk Governance, the proposition that certain forms of systemic risk 
regulation require minimum disclosure thresholds to retain legitimacy; and (iv) Extraterrestrial 
Force Majeure, a doctrinal framework for unidentified, non-state, and non-human aerospace 
phenomena under English contract law and the international space law regime.

The study proceeds doctrinally. It situates these constructs within the Outer Space Treaty 1967, 
the Liability Convention 1972, the Registration Convention 1975, the United Kingdom's Outer 
Space Act 1986 and Space Industry Act 2018, the Solvency II regime as retained in UK law, and 
the comparative regulatory architecture of the remaining Five Eyes jurisdictions. It concludes 
that current orbital insurance arrangements operate on assumptions of informational symmetry 
that are no longer defensible, and proposes a calibrated statutory disclosure obligation, a Five 
Eyes coordination mechanism, and a residual reinsurance backstop as the minimum institutional 
response.
Keywords: space law; insurance regulation; Outer Space Treaty; Solvency II; Five Eyes; 
aerospace disclosure; actuarial governance; force majeure; systemic risk.

detail.abstract: Somalia presents one of the most complex macroeconomic environments in Sub-Saharan Africa. Emerging from decades of civil conflict, state collapse, and humanitarian crises, the Somali economy has demonstrated remarkable informal resilience, driven primarily by remittances, pastoralism, and a thriving services sector operating largely outside formal institutional frameworks. This paper provides a comprehensive macroeconomic overview of Somalia, examining GDP dynamics, inflation pressures, sectoral composition, monetary conditions, fiscal constraints, and the pivotal role of diaspora remittances. detail.abstract:
This monograph develops a physics-informed framework for the governance of congested near-Earth 
orbital space. It argues that the prevailing legal architecture — anchored in the Outer Space Treaty 1967, 
the Liability Convention 1972, the Registration Convention 1975, and a thin lattice of national licensing 
regimes — conceptualises orbital activity as a series of discrete operational acts conducted by sovereign 
or sovereign-affiliated actors in an effectively empty medium. That conceptualisation no longer reflects 
the operational reality of the orbital domain. Mega-constellations, hybrid civil–military architectures, 
autonomous manoeuvring systems, and accumulating debris populations have produced a dynamically 
interacting, instability-prone systemic environment whose risk properties are continuous, cumulative, and 
non-linear.

Drawing on the structural form (though not the formal mathematics) of astrophysical instability models 
— the Toomre criterion, Jeans instability, runaway accretion in planetesimal disks, and migration 
dynamics in protoplanetary systems — the monograph proposes a conceptual architecture in which orbital 
governance is understood as the management of threshold behaviour in a complex adaptive system. The 
framework is applied to four contemporary governance problems: the emerging crisis in orbital insurance 
markets; cascading debris and collision-chain liability under the Liability Convention regime; the collapse 
of the civil–military distinction in hybrid orbital systems with particular attention to NATO and Five Eyes 
architectures; and the rise of inference-based governance under conditions of attribution opacity and 
informational monopoly.

The monograph is anchored in United Kingdom regulatory practice under the Outer Space Act 1986 and 
the Space Industry Act 2018, with comparative analysis of United States, NATO, and Five Eyes 
frameworks. It concludes by proposing six conceptual components of a physics-informed governance 
architecture: dynamic governance thresholds, probabilistic attribution standards, systemic-risk insurance 
pools, orbital congestion indices, sovereign transparency tiers, and autonomous-system oversight 
frameworks. These are presented not as draft regulation but as a methodological re-orientation: a shift 
from conduct-based to system-state governance of the orbital domain.

title: Housing as a Bundled Political Shock: Rent, Wealth, and Voting

detail.title: Housing as a Bundled Political Shock: Rent, Wealth, and Voting
detail.abstract: While the empirical literature documents the association between housing wealth and political behaviour, the structural mechanism through which housing pressure produces mainstream exit is contested. This paper presents a structural contribution: I decompose housing pressure into three substantively distinct margins of household experience that bundle into the same lived situation, namely rent burden, exclusion from housing capital gains among non-owners, and family-financed entry into ownership. I then discipline the behavioural parameters against German wealth distributional, housing-market and electoral moments, and use counterfactual policy experiments to show that the three-margin structure changes the policy ranking. To this end, I develop a calibrated agent-based model with heterogeneity in households (region, tenure, wealth and aspiration) and in regional housing markets. Both forms of heterogeneity are crucial because the three margins are not collinear at the household level, hence an aggregate model cannot separate them. The three margins enter a reference-dependent dissatisfaction process and shape household voting probabilities, which in turn drives the political response to housing-policy interventions. I calibrate the model to 30,000 German households across 16 regions in order to estimate the housing-channel component of mainstream exit around the AfD second-vote share in the 23 February 2025 federal election. The mechanism is then externally stress-tested against UK Brexit voting at the NUTS-1 level in the 2016 referendum. Eight behavioural parameters are disciplined by Simulated Method of Moments (SMM) against twelve German distributional, housing-market and political-economy targets. When simulating five policy counterfactuals over a 25-period horizon, I find that only one of the five counterfactual scenarios reverses the political trajectory: a bundled intervention combining the housing-policy block with a capital-tax-funded redistributive transfer to the bottom half of the wealth distribution. I find that housing instruments operate as complements rather than substitutes: Mietpreisbremse, Wohngeld and supply-side reform, even at full delivery 1 intensity, leave the political channel of mainstream exit open, since the housing-only policy block reaches the rent margin alone and does not address blocked ownership or unequal wealth transmission.

title: Home Production, Skill Heterogeneity and the Labor Wedge

detail.title: Home Production, Skill Heterogeneity and the Labor Wedge
detail.abstract: The labor wedge, the inequivalence between the MRS and MPL, is a measure of market inefficiency and its cyclicality implies fluctuations between consumption, labor supply and employment. To explain it, we write a Beckerian model where non-market consumption, such as home production and leisure, is produced by allocating resources, such as money and time. We find that the labor wedge's distortionary metrics are substantially explained by home production and skill heterogeneity. Specifically, the skill-based money input and skill premium play a primary role and the skill-based time input and skill composition play a secondary role. Furthermore, welfare is procyclical during economic expansion and countercyclical during recessions. Skill heterogeneity not only enhances welfare but also contributes to its stability throughout business cycles. A procyclical fiscal policy customized to each skill level and each non-market sector could effectively eliminate the labor wedge and optimize welfare.

detail.abstract:
This report uses microeconomic theory to study Amouage, an Omani luxury fragrance brand founded in 1983. The analysis covers four main areas: market structure, price elasticity of demand (PED), supply and demand, and government intervention. All data comes from published industry reports, company press releases, and credible news sources.
Amouage operates under monopolistic competition — a market with many competing brands, each selling a distinct product. Thanks to its Omani royal heritage, UNESCO-protected frankincense, and ultra-high concentration (30–40%+), Amouage can charge premium prices of $250–$550 per bottle. In 2025, the brand reached $430M+ in total sales, a +66% increase from the previous year (Business of Fashion, 2026).
A key finding is that Amouage's demand is inelastic, meaning customers are not highly sensitive to price changes. The estimated Price Elasticity of Demand (PED) is approximately −0.3 to −0.5. This indicates that price increases do not lead to a significant drop in sales, allowing Amouage to maintain premium prices without losing most of its customer base (Business Research Insights; Business of Fashion, 2026).
On the supply side, the main challenges are rising raw material costs (oud, Bulgarian rose, and vetiver went up 20–40% in 2024–25) and a production limit of around 25,000 bottles per week. Amouage manages these pressures by owning its own frankincense grove (vertical integration), running a 100% solar-powered factory, and leveraging capital from L'Oréal's minority stake to expand its boutiques from 16 to 25 globally (DataIntelo, 2025; Business of Fashion, 2025a).
Two government interventions are studied: Oman's Vision 2040 industrial policy, which addresses under-investment in positive externalities, and the Oman IP Law framework, which tackles information asymmetry caused by counterfeiting. Finally, four policy recommendations are proposed by government regulators, each addressing a specific market failure.

detail.abstract: The formulation of the category of gradual civic capitulation is part of a line of research oriented toward the analysis of contemporary forms of political legitimation of social deterioration, previously developed in La descomposición de un Estado. Argentina 2023–2025 (Enricci, 2026a) and in Selective State Decomposition under Democratic Continuity (Enricci, 2026b). In this framework, the concept seeks to contribute to the understanding of the mechanisms by which certain processes of economic, institutional and social deterioration manage to sustain persistent levels of electoral legitimacy and symbolic adherence. Gradual civic capitulation is the process by which social sectors electorally and symbolically sustain a political model even when they experience its adverse material effects. It is a dynamic form of reorganization of social expectations in which present deterioration is integrated into common sense as part of horizons associated with order, stability or the promise of future transformation.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the distributional implications of Airbnb income using matched administrative data combining transaction-level tourist tax records, cadastral data, and household tax data from the La Rochelle coastal urban area in France. We conceptualize short-term rentals as a mechanism enabling households to extract an intermittent tourist rent from housing assets. Using a Heckman selection model, we distinguish between participation in Airbnb activity and revenues conditional on participation. The results show that higherincome households are more likely to participate in Airbnb hosting, but that higher revenues are driven primarily by price premium rather than rental intensity. This suggests that Airbnb amplifies unequal returns associated with heterogeneous housing assets rather than differences in hosting effort. At the same time, Airbnb income represents a substantial share of disposable income for some lower-income households. The paper highlights the dual role of short-term rentals as both a mechanism reinforcing income concentration and a source of temporary income buffering.

title: Global Equity Risk Premiums (ERP) & Country Risk Premiums (CRP)

detail.title: Global Equity Risk Premiums (ERP) & Country Risk Premiums (CRP)
detail.abstract: Every valuation rests on a discount rate, and every discount rate rests on a risk premium. When that valuation involves a company operating in Brazil or an acquirer pricing a target in Indonesia, the question of which risk premium to use becomes anything but trivial, investors in these markets bear political instability, violence, corruption, and institutional fragility that mature markets have largely priced away. Ignoring that is not conservatism, it is mispricing. This paper documents the methodology for estimating Equity Risk Premiums and Country Risk Premiums across 174 countries and 9 global regions as of April-May 2026, building explicitly on the framework developed by Professor Aswath Damodaran of NYU Stern, with three methodological refinements: the risk-free rate is derived by netting CDS spreads against Switzerland rather than applying a rating-based default spread, ensuring consistency with the CRP framework; the mature market ERP strips America's full country risk premium rather than its raw sovereign default spread from the implied ERP; the relative volatility multiplier uses indices with balanced exposure across both developed and emerging markets; all through a three-tier hierarchy of CDS spreads, Moody's rating-implied spreads, and Political Risk Service scores. The result is a set of estimates any analyst can use in cross-border valuation without rebuilding the methodology from scratch.

detail.abstract: This article analyses and evaluates Fianna Fáil's 'progressive republican' cross-class ideological strategy between 2011 and 2024 after the economic crisis and electoral collapse in 2011. Drawing on Antonio Gramsci's hegemony, it demonstrates how the party reconstructed strategically 'national-popular' identity (i.e. republicanism) and 'common sense' values (i.e. 'fairness') to attempt to rebuild ideologically a cross-class alliance-the historic foundation of its hegemony. Party leader speeches, party literature and policy documents are analysed to show how its 'progressive republican' collective identity and core values framed a new programme. It argues the strategy yielded a partial recovery but ultimately failed at the implementation stage as it was unable and unwilling to transform substantially the structural effects of Fianna Fáil's previous neoliberal policies. The latter created deep class contradictions and inequalities in housing and health provision for low and median-income workers. This meant the limited concessions actually implemented post-2020 were ineffective in winning their consent. I thus conclude that the era of Fianna Fáil one-party hegemony is finally over. The article also defends class and ideological analysis in the light of this application maintaining against existing scholarship that it can provide insights into Fianna Fáil and wider Irish party politics.

title: Planned Obsolescence and Environmental Law

detail.title: Planned Obsolescence and Environmental Law
detail.abstract:
Planned obsolescence has long been discussed from the perspective of consumer protection and market regulation. Its environmental dimension, however, remains insufficiently explored, particularly regarding the role of public policies that indirectly stimulate unsustainable production models. This paper analyzes the legal paradox created when governments grant fiscal incentives or environmental operating licenses to companies whose business strategies rely on artificially shortened product life cycles. Such practices significantly increase the generation of electronic waste, transferring environmental and economic burdens to municipalities responsible for waste management.
Based on Brazilian environmental law and comparative regulatory frameworks, the study investigates whether current licensing procedures adequately assess the full life cycle of products and whether tax benefits granted without environmental conditionalities are compatible with constitutional principles of sustainable development. The article argues for the incorporation of durability, reparability, and reverse logistics obligations as mandatory criteria in environmental licensing and fiscal incentive programs. Finally, it proposes regulatory alternatives aimed at aligning economic policies with circular economy principles and the polluter-pays doctrine.

title: Market Learning from Sequential Geopolitical Escalations: Evidence from Airline Stocks
affiliations: Bar-Ilan University - Graduate School of Business Administration

detail.title: Market Learning from Sequential Geopolitical Escalations: Evidence from Airline Stocks
detail.abstract: This study examines how financial markets respond to three sequential escalations of conflict with increasing geographic scope: a local conflict in Israel, a regional escalation involving Iran, and a global episode involving the United States. Focusing on the airline industry, which is particularly vulnerable to geopolitical crises, we treat this sequence as a quasi-natural experiment to assess how markets adjust to repeated shocks. Using a sample of 56 publicly traded airlines, we find that greater direct exposure to conflict-related regions is associated with larger immediate negative abnormal returns (ARs), primarily during the local event. Over time, however, this pattern attenuates and partially reverses across groups: Israeli and U.S. firms exhibit greater resilience and stronger recovery, suggesting that initial exposure-based pricing is revised. We find only partial support for the hypothesis that market responses increase monotonically with escalation scope: the global escalation generates the largest and most uniform negative response, whereas the regional escalation yields muted effects despite its broader geographic scope. Across business model categories, exposed low-cost carriers incur larger losses across all three episodes, while non-exposed low-cost carriers are disproportionately affected during the global escalation. Overall, the evidence supports a dynamic adjustment process in which exposure-based pricing is strongest during the initial local shock but weakens as geopolitical shocks broaden. Investors appear to shift from exposurebased pricing to a broader reassessment of industry-wide risk.

title: Log-returns Structure: A Three-dimensional Edge Framework
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Log-returns Structure: A Three-dimensional Edge Framework
detail.abstract:
This paper extends the previously published article: "Log-Returns Structure: Probability, Volatility, Risk, Bias, and Edge in Financial Markets" by presenting a three-dimensional interpretation of financial Edge. The framework is based on decomposing a log-return series into cumulative positive and negative movement components, allowing return to be analyzed not only as a final outcome, but as an internal structure.

The central contribution of the paper is the expansion of Edge from a single measure into three complementary dimensions: Edge relative to total movement, Edge relative to negative movement, and Edge relative to positive movement. These three dimensions provide different perspectives on the same return structure and form a closed mathematical system through the Log-Bias Ratio.

This framework enables a more precise interpretation of return quality. It distinguishes between the efficiency of total movement conversion, return relative to adverse movement, and the degree to which positive movement is retained after negative movement is deducted.

The paper also applies the framework to long and short positions. At the asset level, positive and negative movements describe objective price structure. At the investor level, their economic meaning depends on the direction of exposure. For long positions, negative movement represents adverse movement; for short positions, positive movement becomes the relevant adverse component. The paper further emphasizes that structural symmetry in log-return space does not imply full symmetry in realized wealth, especially for passive short positions.

The proposed framework does not replace classical performance metrics. Rather, it provides a compact structural layer that may complement asset analysis, strategy evaluation, long/short comparison, backtesting diagnostics, and quantitative model construction.

title: Agentic AI Cyber Subversion: The Semantic Layer Integrity Attack as a New Threat Class Against the Reasoning Layer

detail.title: Agentic AI Cyber Subversion: The Semantic Layer Integrity Attack as a New Threat Class Against the Reasoning Layer

detail.abstract:
Agentic AI introduces a cyber risk that does not begin with compromised credentials, poisoned training data, prompt injection, unauthorized tool use, or anomalous output. It begins when an autonomous system resolves the meaning of a regulated term across enterprise systems before execution, and that resolved meaning diverges from the definition the institution authorized. The corrupted object is not the input, the output, the model, the tool call, or the log. It is the resolved operational meaning.

This paper defines Agentic Workflow Subversion as the enterprise risk surface created when reasoning-layer drift propagates across workflows, systems, and control boundaries. It defines the Semantic Layer Integrity Attack (SLIA) as the deliberate adversarial form of that risk: a cross-system integrity attack in which an actor manipulates the semantic conditions under which an agent resolves authorization, eligibility, clearance, risk, or control status, while every contributing system continues to behave correctly. It is a failure of control integrity without system compromise. The attack is cyber-relevant because it produces a clean control record. The network is not breached. The model is not necessarily altered. The prompt may be benign. The tool call may be authorized. The output may be well formed. The audit trail may be complete. Yet execution proceeds under a corrupted operational interpretation that no human or institution authorized.

It situates the attack against existing agent security controls, including identity, workload authentication, prompt and input defenses, tool governance, memory and retrieval controls, output filtering, auditability, and defense-in-depth architectures. It shows that these controls are necessary but incomplete, because they govern the artifacts around agentic reasoning rather than the meaning resolved by the reasoning layer itself. It then maps the gap against current cyber and AI governance taxonomies, including NIST adversarial machine learning, the OWASP agentic AI security corpus, MITRE ATLAS, STRIDE, the Five Eyes agentic AI security guidance, and financial sector supervisory expectations, in the disciplined posture that each framework is authoritative for the scope it declares and the reasoning layer is the adjacent surface it does not directly observe.

The contribution is a cyber threat class definition and a control surface argument. Agentic Workflow Subversion names the risk surface. The Semantic Layer Integrity Attack names its adversarial exploitation path. Semantic Substrate Validation and the Semantic Control Plane (SCP), operating within the broader Agentic Governance Model (AGM), name the runtime governance surface required to detect, constrain, and evidence semantic integrity before execution proceeds. It closes with detection and test conditions, control tailoring, and supervisory implications, so that the threat class is operationally actionable for a cybersecurity function rather than only conceptually defined.

detail.abstract: Although use of generative AI tools has quickly become widespread in education settings, emerging evidence suggests that effects on learning will depend on how that use is supported and guided. This paper reports findings from an original national survey of K-12 school principals designed to measure institutional integration of AI in schools through policies, teacher training, guidance for student use, leadership engagement, and the availability of AI-enabled tools. We find that AI use has spread rapidly across schools, largely as a productivity aid. Students mainly use AI for homework help and writing, while educators primarily use it for lesson planning and administrative tasks. The development of teacher training, guidance, and school policies has lagged adoption. We next document two diffusion gaps across schools: First, lower AI integration is associated with a higher share of disadvantaged students (a one standard deviation increase in disadvantage is associated with a 0.07-0.11σ lower score on an index of AI integration); Second, private and charter schools score 0.23-0.44σ lower on the AI integration index than traditional public schools. Although several surveyed school-level factors strongly predict AI integration, they do little to explain these gaps. Differences in district size account for roughly one-third of the disadvantage gap between public schools. These findings suggest that the factors associated with greater AI integration differ from those needed to narrow disparities in how schools support and guide AI use.

detail.abstract: Export credit agencies play a central role in financing cross-border trade, particularly in destinations where private trade finance is scarce, yet firm-level evidence on how such support shapes export patterns across destination risk environments remains limited. We construct a firm-destination panel for 2011-2023 by linking export credit guarantee records with customs data and exploit within-firm variation in guarantee use across destinations and over time. We document a pronounced destination-risk gradient in the association between export credit guarantees and exports. Guarantees are associated with a substantially higher probability of market entry in higher-risk destinations as classified by the OECD country risk framework, while the corresponding association is markedly smaller in the lowest-risk markets. At the intensive margin, the export elasticity with respect to guarantees is approximately 65% larger in riskier destinations. These patterns are strongest for smaller firms, consistent with tighter external financing constraints. While our empirical design does not rely on quasi-experimental variation, the systematic alignment between the observed heterogeneity and the predictions of trade-finance theory suggests that public export credit support operates primarily through a financing-cost channel, alleviating constraints where private trade finance is scarce.

title: Measuring Decision Procedures under Nonlinear Incentives

detail.title: Measuring Decision Procedures under Nonlinear Incentives
detail.abstract: This paper studies how people articulate decision procedures under nonlinear incentives. In a 2×2 experiment, subjects make choices under piecewise-linear tax schedules that vary the number of brackets in the schedules (bracket count) and the number of marginal tax rate-slopes relevant to optimal choice (slope count). They then provide incentivized free-text explanations in either a Description frame, which asks what they did in the choice task, or a Prescription frame, which asks them what they believe should be done in the choice task. Building on the information-processing approach to adaptive decision-making and the use of Elementary Information Processes (EIP) to measure cognitive effort in choice (Newell and Simon, 1972; Bettman et al., 1990; Payne et al., 1993), I count the EIP operations in subjects' reported procedures as a measure of the cognitive demand of their response to the incentive structure. I find that slope count raises procedural operations after accounting for explanation length, while bracket count does not have a robust effect. EIP count is also meaningfully linked to the reasoning explained by subjects. Explanations consistent with the marginal reasoning principle have the highest EIP count, followed by average rate-based explanations, while all other kinds of explanations have the lowest EIP count. This relationship is supported by subjects' performance in an independent menu-based check of their rule-knowledge. The slope effect appears in both Description and Prescription, with no statistically distinguishable difference across frames, suggesting that subjects recognize the additional demands of the environment in both implemented and identified procedures. Finally, higher EIP count is associated with lower cognitive uncertainty, longer response time, and lower error during the choice task itself. The results show that nonlinear incentives create procedural demands that are visible in what subjects articulate about their decisions, and that these articulated procedures are meaningfully related to rule-knowledge and decision accuracy.

detail.abstract:
The four decades stretching from the Roaring Twenties through the postwar boom were, in environmental terms, a long retreat from the Progressive Era's gains. This chapter traces how law underwrote the physical transformation of America — suburbs, highways, dams, automobiles, chemicals, nuclear power — making the United States simultaneously the world's greatest economic superpower and its greatest polluter.

The era's central paradox is the New Deal. Franklin Roosevelt's administrative revolution built the modern federal bureaucratic state — and built it primarily as an instrument of development. The TVA, the Hoover Dam, the rural electrification programs: these projects flooded ecosystems, displaced communities, and locked in fossil fuel infrastructure whose consequences the planet is still living with. Yet the same administrative machinery, built to facilitate exploitation, would later become the scaffolding on which modern environmental law was constructed. The engine of destruction carried within it the tools of repair.

Federal policy during this era also systematically racialized the "American Dream." FHA mortgage programs, interstate highway routing, and racially restrictive covenants concentrated pollution burdens in communities of color while delivering the benefits of suburbanization almost exclusively to white Americans — a pattern that environmental justice advocates are still fighting decades later.

The chapter closes with the era's accumulating disasters: the Donora death fog of 1948, the proliferation of synthetic chemicals with minimal legal oversight, and the nuclear fallout that would eventually inspire Rachel Carson's generation. Even in the anti-conservation atmosphere of these decades, undercurrents of reform persisted — modest federal experiments, early state air and water regulations, scattered legislative responses to industrial disaster. These inadequate but persistent efforts would prove essential to what came next.

title: Growing Awareness and Ambiguity Attitude

detail.title: Growing Awareness and Ambiguity Attitude
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether prior experience of growing awareness of outcomes influences subsequent attitudes toward ambiguity, and whether any such effect operates beyond elicited first-order beliefs. In a controlled experiment, subjects draw 40 times from an urn under one of two conditions. In the Complete awareness condition, the full support of the urn distribution is known from the outset, while in the Growing awareness condition, subjects discover the support gradually through sampling. After sampling, subjects make matched investment decisions under ambiguity and risk. The central result is a robust interaction between the prior awareness condition and the decision environment on the within-subject difference in investments between the Ambiguity stage and Risk stage. Subjects in the Growing awareness condition who are later assigned to an environment built around outcomes that were frequently encountered during sampling exhibit weaker ambiguity aversion relative to Complete awareness counterparts. The pattern reverses for subjects assigned to the environment built around rarely encountered outcomes during sampling, such that prior exposure to growth in awareness is associated with a substantially lower investment in the Ambiguity stage. The interaction effect of-26.4 (p = 0.011) cents in the baseline specification persists after accounting for elicited beliefs, belief precision, sampling frequencies, and the recency of awareness-expanding discoveries. The findings indicate that awareness history affects ambiguity attitude through a channel not exhausted by beliefs, and that its direction depends on whether the decision environment involves frequent or rare outcomes from prior experience.

detail.abstract: Beginning in the 2000s, as Central and Eastern European countries began to join the EU in earnest, new manufacturing production bases within the EU were established in Central and Eastern Europe. This marked the beginning of a full-scale expansion of Korean companies targeting the EU market. This expansion was concentrated in the V4 (Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia) countries between 2006 and 2007. From the late 2010s until recently, Korean companies’ expansion into Central and Eastern Europe shifted to investments in batteries, electric vehicles, renewable energy, and R&D, shifting investment patterns toward eco-friendly and cutting-edge industries and key supply chains. detail.abstract: This paper revisits the roles of information, security selection, and portfolio construction in active equity management within a Markowitz mean–variance framework. Using data from 2004–2024 across U.S. and global equity markets, the study evaluates regression-based composite models that integrate valuation metrics, earnings forecasts, revisions, breadth, and momentum. Robust estimation methods, including weighted latent root regression (WLRR) and Least Angle Regression (LAR), show that earnings-related variables, particularly composite forecast measures, consistently generate statistically significant return signals. Longstanding enhanced multifactor models deliver higher information coefficients and forecast efficacy than traditional valuation-only approaches. When implemented within mean–variance optimization, these models produce economically meaningful excess returns in MSCI ACWI and Emerging Markets portfolios, even after accounting for transaction costs and data-mining adjustments. Results further indicate that portfolio construction materially amplifies security selection skill, particularly with higher tracking error and active weights. The paper also explores the possibility of improving forecasting results using alternative highdimensional and machine learning methods and finds that robust regression approaches (WLRR and LAR) deliver the highest out-of-sample information coefficients. These findings, along with related published research, support the notion that disciplined, interpretable methods remain highly competitive tools for equity forecasting during much of the last 30 years. Finally, the analysis shows that expanding the investment universe to include a more comprehensive set of global stocks with earnings forecasts improves Sharpe and information ratios, underscoring the benefits of broad, information-rich opportunity sets and robust statistical modeling in active management.

title: Spillover Effects of Timelier Loan Loss Recognition by Banks on Borrowers’ Cross-Border Borrowing

detail.title: Spillover Effects of Timelier Loan Loss Recognition by Banks on Borrowers’ Cross-Border Borrowing
detail.abstract: The transition from the incurred credit loss model to the expected credit loss model in bank accounting for loan losses requires domestic banks to monitor borrowers’ credit quality more closely and recognize expected loan losses more promptly. Using a difference-in-differences analysis of syndicated loans from 62 countries, our study finds that after the transition, domestic borrowers increase their cross-border borrowing. Additional evidence indicates that this effect is driven by reduced credit supply and more restrictive covenants imposed by domestic banks. The effect is stronger when the transition is likely to increase banks’ loan loss provisions, as well as among borrowers with greater cross-border borrowing experience, closer linguistic ties with foreign lenders, or limited access to domestic bond markets. Our study is the first to show that cross-country differences in bank accounting can affect firms’ cross-border borrowing.
